<p id="mwGg">The <b id="mwGw">cat</b> (<i id="mwHA"><b id="mwHQ">Felis catus</b></i>), also called <b id="mwHg">domestic cat</b> and <b id="mwHw">house cat</b>, is a small domesticated <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivore" title="Carnivore" id="mwIA">carnivorous</a> mammal. It is a member of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felidae" title="Felidae" id="mwIQ">Felidae</a>, the family of mammals in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_(taxonomy)" title="Order (taxonomy)" id="mwIg">order</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnivora" title="Carnivora" id="mwIw">Carnivora</a> also colloquially referred to as cats. It is an <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obligate_carnivore" title="Obligate carnivore" class="mw-redirect" id="mwJA">obligate carnivore</a>, requiring a predominantly meat-based diet. Its retractable <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claw" title="Claw" id="mwJQ">claws</a> are adapted to killing small prey species such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mice" title="Mice" class="mw-redirect" id="mwJg">mice</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rat" title="Rat" id="mwJw">rats</a>. It has a strong, flexible body, quick <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reflex" title="Reflex" id="mwKA">reflexes</a>, and sharp teeth, and its <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Night_vision" title="Night vision" id="mwKQ">night vision</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sense_of_smell" title="Sense of smell" id="mwKg">sense of smell</a> are well developed. It is a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_species" title="Social species" class="mw-redirect" id="mwKw">social species</a>, but a solitary hunter and a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crepuscular" title="Crepuscular" class="mw-redirect" id="mwLA">crepuscular</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Predator" title="Predator" class="mw-redirect" id="mwLQ">predator</a>.
<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_communication" title="Cat communication" id="mwLg">Cat communication</a> includes <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meow" title="Meow" id="mwLw">meowing</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purr" title="Purr" id="mwMA">purring</a>, trilling, <a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hiss" title="wiktionary:hiss" class="extiw" id="mwMQ">hissing</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growling" title="Growling" id="mwMg">growling</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/grunt" title="wiktionary:grunt" class="extiw" id="mwMw">grunting</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_body_language" title="Cat body language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwNA">body language</a>. It can hear sounds too faint or too high in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frequency" title="Frequency" id="mwNQ">frequency</a> for human ears, such as those made by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_mammal" title="Small mammal" id="mwNg">small mammals</a>. It secretes and perceives <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheromone" title="Pheromone" id="mwNw">pheromones</a>. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_intelligence" title="Cat intelligence" id="mwOA">Cat intelligence</a> is evident in its ability to adapt, learn through observation, and solve problems. The domestic cat is the only <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication" title="Domestication" id="mwOQ">domesticated</a> <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Species" title="Species" id="mwOg">species</a> of the family Felidae. </p>

<p id="mwOw">Advances in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology" title="Archaeology" id="mwPA">archaeology</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetics" title="Genetics" id="mwPQ">genetics</a> have shown that the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_the_cat" title="Domestication of the cat" id="mwPg">domestication of the cat</a> started in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_East" title="Near East" id="mwPw">Near East</a> around 7500 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BCE" title="BCE" class="mw-redirect" id="mwQA">BCE</a>. Today, the domestic cat occurs across the globe and is valued by humans for companionship and its ability to kill <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermin" title="Vermin" id="mwQQ">vermin</a>. It is commonly kept as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pet" title="Pet" id="mwQg">pet</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_cat" title="Working cat" id="mwQw">working cat</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedigreed_cat" title="Pedigreed cat" class="mw-redirect" id="mwRA">pedigreed cat</a> shown at <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_fancy" title="Cat fancy" id="mwRQ">cat fancy</a> events. Out of the estimated 600<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwRg"> </span>million domestic cats worldwide, 400<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwRw"> </span>million reside in Asia, including 58<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwSA"> </span>million in China. About 73.8<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwSQ"> </span>million cats are estimated to live in the United States, and about 10.9<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwSg"> </span>million cats in the United Kingdom. It also ranges freely as a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_cat" title="Feral cat" id="mwSw">feral cat</a>, avoiding human contact. Pet abandonment contributes to increasing of the global feral cat population, which has driven the decline of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bird" title="Bird" id="mwTA">bird</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal" title="Mammal" id="mwTQ">mammal</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptile" title="Reptile" id="mwTg">reptile</a> species. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_population_control" title="Animal population control" class="mw-redirect" id="mwTw">Population control</a> includes <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaying" title="Spaying" class="mw-redirect" id="mwUA">spaying</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutering" title="Neutering" id="mwUQ">neutering</a>.</p>

<section data-mw-section-id="4" id="mwAYA" aria-labelledby="Domestication"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Domestication">Domestication</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt187" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAYE" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"See also","href":"./Template:See_also"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Domestication of the cat"},"2":{"wt":"Cats in ancient Egypt"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt188" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt187" id="mwAYI">See also: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_the_cat" title="Domestication of the cat">Domestication of the cat</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cats_in_ancient_Egypt" title="Cats in ancient Egypt">Cats in ancient Egypt</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAYM"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomb_of_Nakht_(7).jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAYQ"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tomb_of_Nakht_(7).jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Tomb_of_Nakht_%287%29.jpg/250px-Tomb_of_Nakht_%287%29.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="761" data-file-height="828" data-file-type="bitmap" height="272" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Tomb_of_Nakht_%287%29.jpg/500px-Tomb_of_Nakht_%287%29.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAYU"></a><figcaption id="mwAYY">A cat eats a fish under a chair, in a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mural" title="Mural" id="mwAYc">mural</a> in an Egyptian tomb dating to the 15th century BCE.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAYg">It was long thought that the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_the_cat" title="Domestication of the cat" id="mwAYk">domestication of the cat</a> began in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt" title="Ancient Egypt" id="mwAYo">ancient Egypt</a>, where cats were venerated from around 3100 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Before_Common_Era" title="Before Common Era" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAYs">BCE</a>.<sup about="#mwt191" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-39" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-39"}}"><a href="#cite_note-39" id="mwAYw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAY0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAY4">[</span>38<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAY8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt194" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-40" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-40"}}"><a href="#cite_note-40" id="mwAZA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZI">[</span>39<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZM">]</span></span></a></sup> However, the earliest known indication for the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taming" title="Taming" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAZQ">taming</a> of an African wildcat was <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Excavation_(archaeology)" title="Excavation (archaeology)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAZU">excavated</a> close by a human <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic" title="Neolithic" id="mwAZY">Neolithic</a> grave in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shillourokambos" title="Shillourokambos" id="mwAZc">Shillourokambos</a>, southern <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyprus" title="Cyprus" id="mwAZg">Cyprus</a>, dating to about 7500–7200 BCE. Since there is no evidence of native mammalian <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauna" title="Fauna" id="mwAZk">fauna</a> on Cyprus, the inhabitants of this village most likely brought the cat and other wild mammals to the island from the West Asian mainland.<sup about="#mwt197" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Vigne_al2004_41-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Vigne_al2004"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Vigne_al2004-41"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Vigne_al2004-41" id="mwAZo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAZs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZw">[</span>40<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAZ0">]</span></span></a></sup> Scientists therefore assume that African wildcats were attracted to early human settlements in the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertile_Crescent" title="Fertile Crescent" id="mwAZ4">Fertile Crescent</a> by rodents, in particular the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_mouse" title="House mouse" id="mwAZ8">house mouse</a> (<i id="mwAaA">Mus musculus</i>), and were tamed by Neolithic farmers. This <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutualism_(biology)" title="Mutualism (biology)" id="mwAaE">mutual</a> relationship between early farmers and tamed cats lasted thousands of years. As <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agricultural_practices" title="Agricultural practices" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAaI">agricultural practices</a> spread, so did tame and domesticated cats.<sup about="#mwt200" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007_38-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007-38"}}"><a href="#cite_note-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007-38" id="mwAaM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAaQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaU">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAaY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt204" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Driscoll_al2009_42-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Driscoll_al2009"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Driscoll_al2009-42"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Driscoll_al2009-42" id="mwAac"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAag"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAak">[</span>41<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAao">]</span></span></a></sup> Wildcats of Egypt contributed to the maternal <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gene_pool" title="Gene pool" id="mwAas">gene pool</a> of the domestic cat at a later time.<sup about="#mwt207" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-OttoniVan_Neer2017_43-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"OttoniVan Neer2017"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-OttoniVan_Neer2017-43"}}"><a href="#cite_note-OttoniVan_Neer2017-43" id="mwAaw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAa0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAa4">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAa8">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAbA">The earliest known evidence for the occurrence of the domestic cat in Greece dates to around 1200 BCE. Greek, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenicia" title="Phoenicia" id="mwAbE">Phoenician</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthaginia" title="Carthaginia" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAbI">Carthaginian</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etrusca" title="Etrusca" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAbM">Etruscan</a> traders introduced it to southern Europe.<sup about="#mwt210" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Faure2009_44-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Faure2009"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Faure2009-44"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Faure2009-44" id="mwAbQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbY">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbc">]</span></span></a></sup> By the 5th century BCE, it was a familiar animal around settlements in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia" id="mwAbg">Magna Graecia</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruria" title="Etruria" id="mwAbk">Etruria</a>.<sup about="#mwt213" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-45" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-45"}}"><a href="#cite_note-45" id="mwAbo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAbs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAbw">[</span>44<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAb0">]</span></span></a></sup> During the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire" title="Roman Empire" id="mwAb4">Roman Empire</a>, it was introduced to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsica" title="Corsica" id="mwAb8">Corsica</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sardinia" title="Sardinia" id="mwAcA">Sardinia</a>.<sup about="#mwt216" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Vigne1992_46-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Vigne1992"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Vigne1992-46"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Vigne1992-46" id="mwAcE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcM">[</span>45<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAcQ">]</span></span></a></sup> By the end of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire" title="Western Roman Empire" id="mwAcU">Western Roman Empire</a> in the 5th century, the Egyptian domestic cat lineage had arrived in a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_Sea" title="Baltic Sea" id="mwAcY">Baltic Sea</a> port in northern Germany.<sup about="#mwt217" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-OttoniVan_Neer2017_43-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"OttoniVan Neer2017"}}"><a href="#cite_note-OttoniVan_Neer2017-43" id="mwAcc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAcg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAck">[</span>42<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAco">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAcs">The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopard_cat" title="Leopard cat" id="mwAcw">leopard cat</a> (<i id="mwAc0">Prionailurus bengalensis</i>) was <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamed" title="Tamed" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAc4">tamed</a> independently in China around 5500 BCE. This line of a partially domesticated cat left no trace in the domestic cat populations of today.<sup about="#mwt220" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-47" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-47"}}"><a href="#cite_note-47" id="mwAc8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdE">[</span>46<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAdM">During domestication, cats have undergone only minor changes in anatomy and behavior, and they are still capable of surviving in the wild. Several natural behaviors and characteristics of wildcats may have <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preadaptation" title="Preadaptation" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAdQ">pre-adapted</a> them for domestication as pets. These traits include their small size, social nature, obvious body language, love of play, and high intelligence. Their rigorous grooming habits and instinct to bury their bodily waste make them generally much less messy than other domesticated animals. Captive <i id="mwAdU"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leopardus" title="Leopardus" id="mwAdY">Leopardus</a></i> cats may also display affectionate behavior toward humans but are not domesticated.<sup about="#mwt223" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-CameronBeaumont_48-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"CameronBeaumont"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-CameronBeaumont-48"}}"><a href="#cite_note-CameronBeaumont-48" id="mwAdc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdk">[</span>47<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAdo">]</span></span></a></sup> House cats may mate with feral cats.<sup about="#mwt226" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bradshaw1999_49-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bradshaw1999"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bradshaw1999-49"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bradshaw1999-49" id="mwAds"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAdw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAd0">[</span>48<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAd4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAd8">The development of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_breeds" title="Cat breeds" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAeA">cat breeds</a> started in the mid-19th century.<sup about="#mwt229" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-50" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-50"}}"><a href="#cite_note-50" id="mwAeE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAeI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeM">[</span>49<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeQ">]</span></span></a></sup> An analysis of the domestic cat <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genome" title="Genome" id="mwAeU">genome</a> revealed that the ancestral wildcat genome was significantly altered in the process of domestication, as specific <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutation" title="Mutation" id="mwAeY">mutations</a> were selected to develop cat breeds.<sup about="#mwt232" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-51" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-51"}}"><a href="#cite_note-51" id="mwAec"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAeg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAek">[</span>50<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAeo">]</span></span></a></sup> Most breeds are founded on random-bred domestic cats; <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_diversity" title="Genetic diversity" id="mwAes">genetic diversity</a> of these breeds varies between regions, and is lowest in purebred populations, which show more than 20 deleterious <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_disorder" title="Genetic disorder" id="mwAew">genetic disorders</a>.<sup about="#mwt235" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Lipinski_52-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Lipinski"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Lipinski-52"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Lipinski-52" id="mwAe0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAe4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAe8">[</span>51<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfA">]</span></span></a></sup>
<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Felid_hybrid#Domestic_cat_and_hybridization" title="Felid hybrid" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAfE">Hybridization between domestic and other Felinae species</a> is also possible, producing hybrids such as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kellas_cat" title="Kellas cat" id="mwAfI">Kellas cat</a> in Scotland.<sup about="#mwt236" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Oliveira_53-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Oliveira"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Oliveira-53" id="mwAfM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAfQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfU">[</span>52<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt239" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-54" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-54"}}"><a href="#cite_note-54" id="mwAfc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAfg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfk">[</span>53<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAfo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="5" id="mwAfs" aria-labelledby="Characteristics"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Characteristics">Characteristics</h2></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt240" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAfw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat anatomy"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt241" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt240" id="mwAf0">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_anatomy" title="Cat anatomy">Cat anatomy</a></div>

<section data-mw-section-id="6" id="mwAf4" aria-labelledby="Size"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Size">Size</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAf8"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAgA"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg/500px-Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg.png" decoding="async" data-file-width="1040" data-file-height="432" data-file-type="drawing" height="141" width="340" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg/960px-Scheme_cat_anatomy.svg.png 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.35" id="mwAgE"></a><figcaption id="mwAgI">Diagram of the general <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatomy" title="Anatomy" id="mwAgM">anatomy</a> of a male domestic cat</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAgQ">The domestic cat has a smaller <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skull" title="Skull" id="mwAgU">skull</a> and shorter bones than the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_wildcat" title="European wildcat" id="mwAgY">European wildcat</a>.<sup about="#mwt248" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-OConnor_55-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"OConnor"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-OConnor-55"}}"><a href="#cite_note-OConnor-55" id="mwAgc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAgg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgk">[</span>54<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAgo">]</span></span></a></sup> It averages about <span about="#mwt242" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAgs" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"46"},"2":{"wt":"cm"}},"i":0}}]}">46</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt242"> </span><span about="#mwt242">cm (18</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt242"> </span><span about="#mwt242">in)</span> in head-to-body length and <span about="#mwt243" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAgw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"23"},"2":{"wt":"-"},"3":{"wt":"25"},"4":{"wt":"cm"}},"i":0}}]}">23–25</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt243"> </span><span about="#mwt243">cm (9.1–9.8</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt243"> </span><span about="#mwt243">in)</span> in height, with about <span about="#mwt244" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAg0" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"30"},"2":{"wt":"cm"}},"i":0}}]}">30</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt244"> </span><span about="#mwt244">cm (12</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt244"> </span><span about="#mwt244">in)</span> long tails. Males are larger than females.<sup about="#mwt251" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-WCoW_56-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"WCoW"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-WCoW-56"}}"><a href="#cite_note-WCoW-56" id="mwAg4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAg8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhA">[</span>55<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhE">]</span></span></a></sup> Adult domestic cats typically weigh <span about="#mwt245" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAhI" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"4"},"2":{"wt":"-"},"3":{"wt":"5"},"4":{"wt":"kg"}},"i":0}}]}">4–5</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt245"> </span><span about="#mwt245">kg (8.8–11.0</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt245"> </span><span about="#mwt245">lb)</span>.<sup about="#mwt252" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Mattern_31-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Mattern"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Mattern-31" id="mwAhM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAhQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhU">[</span>30<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAhY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="7" id="mwAhc" aria-labelledby="Skeleton"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Skeleton">Skeleton</h3></div>
<p id="mwAhg">Cats have seven <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cervical_vertebrae" title="Cervical vertebrae" id="mwAhk">cervical vertebrae</a> (as do most <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal" title="Mammal" id="mwAho">mammals</a>); 13 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thoracic_vertebrae" title="Thoracic vertebrae" id="mwAhs">thoracic vertebrae</a> (humans have 12); seven <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lumbar_vertebrae" title="Lumbar vertebrae" id="mwAhw">lumbar vertebrae</a> (humans have five); three <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrum" title="Sacrum" id="mwAh0">sacral vertebrae</a> (as do most mammals, but humans have five); and a variable number of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caudal_vertebrae" title="Caudal vertebrae" id="mwAh4">caudal vertebrae</a> in the tail (humans have only three to five vestigial caudal vertebrae, fused into an internal <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coccyx" title="Coccyx" id="mwAh8">coccyx</a>).<sup about="#mwt257" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Walker_57-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Walker"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Walker-57"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Walker-57" id="mwAiA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAiE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiI">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAiM">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt253" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAiQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"11"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 11"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>11<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> The extra lumbar and thoracic vertebrae account for the cat's spinal mobility and flexibility. Attached to the spine are 13 ribs, the shoulder, and the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelvis" title="Pelvis" id="mwAiU">pelvis</a>.<sup about="#mwt258" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Walker_57-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Walker"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Walker-57" id="mwAiY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAic"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAig">[</span>56<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAik">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt254" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAio" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"16"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 16"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>16<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> Unlike human arms, cat forelimbs are attached to the shoulder by free-floating <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clavicle" title="Clavicle" id="mwAis">clavicle</a> bones which allow them to pass their body through any space into which they can fit their head.<sup about="#mwt261" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Gillis_2002_58-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Gillis 2002"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Gillis_2002-58"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Gillis_2002-58" id="mwAiw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAi0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAi4">[</span>57<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAi8">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="8" id="mwAjA" aria-labelledby="Skull"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Skull">Skull</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAjE"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_skull.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAjI"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_skull.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Cat_skull.jpg/250px-Cat_skull.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="818" data-file-height="578" data-file-type="bitmap" height="127" width="180" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Cat_skull.jpg/500px-Cat_skull.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.7" id="mwAjM"></a><figcaption id="mwAjQ">Cat skull</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAjU">The cat skull is unusual among mammals in having very large <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_socket" title="Eye socket" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAjY">eye sockets</a> and a powerful specialized jaw.<sup about="#mwt265" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Case_59-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Case"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Case-59"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Case-59" id="mwAjc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAjg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjk">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAjo">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt262" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAjs" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"35"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 35"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>35<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> Two long <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canine_tooth" title="Canine tooth" id="mwAjw">canine teeth</a> for killing and tearing prey can stab between two of the prey's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertebra" title="Vertebra" id="mwAj0">vertebrae</a> and sever its <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spinal_cord" title="Spinal cord" id="mwAj4">spinal cord</a>, causing <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paralysis" title="Paralysis" id="mwAj8">paralysis</a> and death.<sup about="#mwt268" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Smith1992_60-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Smith1992"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Smith1992-60"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Smith1992-60" id="mwAkA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkI">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkM">]</span></span></a></sup> Compared to other felines, domestic cats have narrowly spaced canine teeth relative to the size of their jaw, which is an adaptation to their preferred prey of small rodents, which have small vertebrae.<sup about="#mwt269" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Smith1992_60-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Smith1992"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Smith1992-60" id="mwAkQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAkU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkY">[</span>59<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAkc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAkg">The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premolar" title="Premolar" id="mwAkk">premolar</a> and first <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molar_(tooth)" title="Molar (tooth)" id="mwAko">molar</a> together compose the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnassial" title="Carnassial" id="mwAks">carnassial</a> pair on each side of the mouth, which efficiently shears meat into small pieces, like a pair of scissors. These are vital in feeding, because cats' small molars cannot chew food effectively, and cats are largely incapable of mastication.<sup about="#mwt271" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Case_59-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Case"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Case-59" id="mwAkw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAk0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAk4">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAk8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt270" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAlA" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"37"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 37"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>37<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> Cats tend to have better dental health than most humans, with decay generally less likely because of a thicker protective layer of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tooth_enamel" title="Tooth enamel" id="mwAlE">enamel</a>, a less damaging saliva, less retention of food particles between teeth, and a diet mostly devoid of sugar. Nonetheless, they are subject to occasional tooth loss and infection.<sup about="#mwt274" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Carr1978_61-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Carr1978"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Carr1978-61"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Carr1978-61" id="mwAlI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAlM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAlQ">[</span>60<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAlU">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="9" id="mwAlY" aria-labelledby="Claws"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Claws">Claws</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAlc"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_claw_closeup.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAlg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_claw_closeup.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Cat_claw_closeup.jpg/250px-Cat_claw_closeup.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1282" data-file-height="960" data-file-type="bitmap" height="135" width="180" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/03/Cat_claw_closeup.jpg/500px-Cat_claw_closeup.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.7" id="mwAlk"></a><figcaption id="mwAlo">Cat's claw</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAls">Cats have protractible and retractable claws.<sup about="#mwt277" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Kitchener2010_62-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Kitchener2010"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Kitchener2010-62"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Kitchener2010-62" id="mwAlw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAl0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAl4">[</span>61<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAl8">]</span></span></a></sup> In their normal, relaxed position, the claws are sheathed with the skin and fur around the paw's toe pads. This keeps the claws sharp by preventing wear from contact with the ground and allows for the silent stalking of prey. The claws on the forefeet are typically sharper than those on the hindfeet.<sup about="#mwt280" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Armes_1900_63-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Armes 1900"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Armes_1900-63"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Armes_1900-63" id="mwAmA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmI">[</span>62<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmM">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats can voluntarily extend their claws, such as in hunting, fighting, climbing, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneading_(cats)" title="Kneading (cats)" id="mwAmQ">kneading</a>, or for extra traction on soft surfaces. Cats shed the outside layer of their claw sheaths when scratching rough surfaces.<sup about="#mwt283" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-pmid19422432_64-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"pmid19422432"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-pmid19422432-64"}}"><a href="#cite_note-pmid19422432-64" id="mwAmU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAmY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmc">[</span>63<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAmg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAmk">Most cats have five claws on their front paws and four on their rear paws. The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewclaw" title="Dewclaw" id="mwAmo">dewclaw</a> is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proximal" title="Proximal" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAms">proximal</a> to the other claws. More proximally is a protrusion which appears to be a sixth "finger". This special feature of the front paws on the inside of the wrists has no function in normal walking but is thought to be an antiskidding device used while jumping. Some cat breeds are prone to having extra digits ("<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polydactyl_cat" title="Polydactyl cat" id="mwAmw">polydactyly</a>").<sup about="#mwt286" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Danforth1947_65-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Danforth1947"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Danforth1947-65"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Danforth1947-65" id="mwAm0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAm4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAm8">[</span>64<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnA">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="10" id="mwAnE" aria-labelledby="Ambulation"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Ambulation">Ambulation</h3></div>
<p id="mwAnI">The cat is <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digitigrade" title="Digitigrade" id="mwAnM">digitigrade</a>. It walks on the toes, with the bones of the feet making up the lower part of the visible leg.<sup about="#mwt289" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Pocock1917_66-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Pocock1917"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Pocock1917-66"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Pocock1917-66" id="mwAnQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAnU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnY">[</span>65<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnc">]</span></span></a></sup> Unlike most mammals, it uses a "pacing" <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gait" title="Gait" id="mwAng">gait</a> that alternates both legs together on each side. It registers directly by placing each hind paw close to the track of the corresponding fore paw, minimizing noise and visible tracks. This also provides sure footing for hind paws when navigating rough terrain. As it speeds up from walking to trotting, its gait changes to a "diagonal" gait: The diagonally opposite hind and fore legs move simultaneously.<sup about="#mwt292" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Christensen_2004_67-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Christensen 2004"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Christensen_2004-67"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Christensen_2004-67" id="mwAnk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAno"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAns">[</span>66<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAnw">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="11" id="mwAn0" aria-labelledby="Balance"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Balance">Balance</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAn4"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_in_tree03.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAn8"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_in_tree03.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Cat_in_tree03.jpg/250px-Cat_in_tree03.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1600" data-file-height="1067" data-file-type="bitmap" height="167" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f8/Cat_in_tree03.jpg/500px-Cat_in_tree03.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwAoA"></a><figcaption id="mwAoE">A cat is perched on a tree branch, having climbed up for exploration, escape, or hunting.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAoI">Cats are generally fond of perching in high places. This may be a concealed hunting site such as a tree branch, for domestic cats to pounce upon prey. They favor a superior observation point over territory. A cat falling from up to <span about="#mwt293" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAoM" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"3"},"2":{"wt":"m"},"3":{"wt":"ft"},"abbr":{"wt":"on"}},"i":0}}]}">3</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt293"> </span><span about="#mwt293">m (9.8</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt293"> </span><span about="#mwt293">ft)</span> can right itself and land on its paws.<sup about="#mwt296" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Kent_et_al._2010_68-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Kent et al. 2010"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Kent_et_al._2010-68"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Kent_et_al._2010-68" id="mwAoQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAoU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoY">[</span>67<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAoc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwAog">During a lofty fall, a cat reflexively twists and rights itself to land on its feet using its acute sense of balance and flexibility. This reflex is known as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_righting_reflex" title="Cat righting reflex" id="mwAok">cat righting reflex</a>.<sup about="#mwt300" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-69" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-69"}}"><a href="#cite_note-69" id="mwAoo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAos"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAow">[</span>68<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAo0">]</span></span></a></sup> A cat always rights itself in the same way, and it has enough time in falls of at least <span about="#mwt297" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAo4" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"90"},"2":{"wt":"cm"},"3":{"wt":"ft"},"abbr":{"wt":"on"}},"i":0}}]}">90</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt297"> </span><span about="#mwt297">cm (3.0</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt297"> </span><span about="#mwt297">ft)</span>.<sup about="#mwt304" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Nguyen_1998_70-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Nguyen 1998"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Nguyen_1998-70"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Nguyen_1998-70" id="mwAo8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwApA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApE">[</span>69<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApI">]</span></span></a></sup> This has been investigated as the "<a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falling_cat_problem" title="Falling cat problem" id="mwApM">falling cat problem</a>".<sup about="#mwt307" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-71" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-71"}}"><a href="#cite_note-71" id="mwApQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwApU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApY">[</span>70<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwApc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="12" id="mwApg" aria-labelledby="Coats"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Coats">Coats</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt308" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwApk" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat coat genetics"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt309" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt308" id="mwApo">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_coat_genetics" title="Cat coat genetics">Cat coat genetics</a></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt310" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAps" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"See also","href":"./Template:See_also"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Tabby cat"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt311" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt310" id="mwApw">See also: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabby_cat" title="Tabby cat">Tabby cat</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAp0"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nursing_Cat_01.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAp4"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nursing_Cat_01.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Nursing_Cat_01.jpg/250px-Nursing_Cat_01.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1440" data-file-height="1800" data-file-type="bitmap" height="225" width="180" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/71/Nursing_Cat_01.jpg/500px-Nursing_Cat_01.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.7" id="mwAp8"></a><figcaption id="mwAqA">Mother cat with her different-colored offspring</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAqE">The domestic cat genes <i id="mwAqI"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MC1R" title="MC1R" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAqM">MC1R</a></i> and <i id="mwAqQ"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agouti-signaling_protein" title="Agouti-signaling protein" id="mwAqU">ASIP</a></i> allow color variety in the coat. The feline <i id="mwAqY">ASIP</i> gene consists of three coding exons.<sup about="#mwt314" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-72" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-72"}}"><a href="#cite_note-72" id="mwAqc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAqg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAqk">[</span>71<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAqo">]</span></span></a></sup> Three novel <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsatellite" title="Microsatellite" id="mwAqs">microsatellite</a> markers linked to <i id="mwAqw">ASIP</i> were isolated from a domestic cat BAC <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clone_(cell_biology)" title="Clone (cell biology)" id="mwAq0">clone</a> containing this gene to perform <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linkage_analysis" title="Linkage analysis" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAq4">linkage analysis</a> on 89 domestic cats segregated for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanism" title="Melanism" id="mwAq8">melanism</a>. The domestic cat family demonstrated a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosegregation" title="Cosegregation" id="mwArA">cosegregation</a> between the <i id="mwArE">ASIP</i> allele and black coloration of the coat.<sup about="#mwt317" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-73" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-73"}}"><a href="#cite_note-73" id="mwArI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwArM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArQ">[</span>72<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwArU">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="13" id="mwArY" aria-labelledby="Diet"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Diet">Diet</h3></div>
<p id="mwArc">The cat is an obligate carnivore and has adapted to a low-fibre highly digestible meat diet. Cats have fewer <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enzyme" title="Enzyme" id="mwArg">enzymes</a> capable of metabolising <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbohydrates" title="Carbohydrates" class="mw-redirect" id="mwArk">carbohydrates</a> compared to omnivores. The cat lacks the ability to convert <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carotenoids" title="Carotenoids" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAro">carotenoids</a> to vitamin A; has an inability to synthesise enough vitamin D; inability to synthesise <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niacin" title="Niacin" class="mw-redirect" id="mwArs">niacin</a> from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tryptophan" title="Tryptophan" id="mwArw">tryptophan</a>; inability to synthesise <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cysteine" title="Cysteine" id="mwAr0">cysteine</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citrulline" title="Citrulline" id="mwAr4">citrulline</a>, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Methionine" title="Methionine" id="mwAr8">methionine</a>; lacks <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucokinase" title="Glucokinase" id="mwAsA">glucokinase</a> activity; and an intolerance to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamic_acid" title="Glutamic acid" id="mwAsE">glutamic acid</a> (which is low in animal tissue and high in plant matter). <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taurine" title="Taurine" id="mwAsI">Taurine</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arginine" title="Arginine" id="mwAsM">arginine</a> are essential for cats. Due to the inability to synthesise adequate amounts of citrulline a single meal lacking in arginine can be fatal to a cat. Cats cannot produce enough taurine and require dietary taurine; a lack of taurine will cause a cat to develop <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dilated_cardiomyopathy" title="Dilated cardiomyopathy" id="mwAsQ">dilated cardiomyopathy</a>. Commercial cat diets historically were lacking in taurine and dilated cardiomyopathy was a common issue until it was linked to taurine deficiency in a 1987 study.<sup about="#mwt320" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Fascetti_2023_74-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Fascetti_2023"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Fascetti_2023-74"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Fascetti_2023-74" id="mwAsU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAsY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAsc">[</span>73<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAsg">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="14" id="mwAsk" aria-labelledby="Senses"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Senses">Senses</h2></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt321" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAso" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat senses"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt322" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt321" id="mwAss">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_senses" title="Cat senses">Cat senses</a></div>

<section data-mw-section-id="15" id="mwAsw" aria-labelledby="Vision"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Vision">Vision</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwAs0"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwAs4"><img alt="A tabby cat with a third, translucent eyelid covering part of either eye" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg/250px-Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="3000" data-file-height="4000" data-file-type="bitmap" height="240" width="180" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/12/Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg/500px-Tabby_cat_with_visible_nictitating_membrane.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.7" id="mwAs8"></a><figcaption id="mwAtA">A cat's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane" title="Nictitating membrane" id="mwAtE">nictitating membrane</a> is exposed as it blinks.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwAtI">Cats have excellent night vision and can see at one sixth the light level required for human vision.<sup about="#mwt324" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Case_59-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Case"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Case-59" id="mwAtM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAtQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAtU">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAtY">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt323" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAtc" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"43"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 43"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>43<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> This is partly the result of cat eyes having a <i id="mwAtg"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapetum_lucidum" title="Tapetum lucidum" id="mwAtk">tapetum lucidum</a></i>, which reflects any light that passes through the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retina" title="Retina" id="mwAto">retina</a> back into the eye, thereby increasing the eye's sensitivity to dim light.<sup about="#mwt327" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-75" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-75"}}"><a href="#cite_note-75" id="mwAts"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAtw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAt0">[</span>74<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAt4">]</span></span></a></sup> Large pupils are an adaptation to dim light. The domestic cat has <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pupil#In_other_animals" title="Pupil" id="mwAt8">slit pupils</a>, which allow it to focus bright light without <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chromatic_aberration" title="Chromatic aberration" id="mwAuA">chromatic aberration</a>.<sup about="#mwt330" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-76" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-76"}}"><a href="#cite_note-76" id="mwAuE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAuI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuM">[</span>75<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuQ">]</span></span></a></sup> At low light, a cat's pupils expand to cover most of the exposed surface of its eyes.<sup about="#mwt333" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-77" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-77"}}"><a href="#cite_note-77" id="mwAuU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAuY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAuc">[</span>76<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAug">]</span></span></a></sup> The domestic cat has rather poor <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_vision" title="Color vision" id="mwAuk">color vision</a> and only two types of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cone_cell" title="Cone cell" id="mwAuo">cone cells</a>, optimized for sensitivity to blue and yellowish green; its ability to distinguish between red and green is limited.<sup about="#mwt336" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-78" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-78"}}"><a href="#cite_note-78" id="mwAus"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAuw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAu0">[</span>77<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAu4">]</span></span></a></sup> A response to middle wavelengths from a system other than the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_cell" title="Rod cell" id="mwAu8">rod cells</a> might be due to a third type of cone. This appears to be an adaptation to low light levels rather than representing true <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichromacy" title="Trichromacy" id="mwAvA">trichromatic</a> vision.<sup about="#mwt339" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-79" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-79"}}"><a href="#cite_note-79" id="mwAvE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvM">[</span>78<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAvQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats have a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nictitating_membrane" title="Nictitating membrane" id="mwAvU">nictitating membrane</a>, allowing them to blink without hindering their vision.</p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="16" id="mwAvY" aria-labelledby="Hearing"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Hearing">Hearing</h3></div>
<p id="mwAvc">The domestic cat's hearing is most acute in the range of 500<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAvg"> </span><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hz" title="Hz" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAvk">Hz</a> to 32<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAvo"> </span>kHz.<sup about="#mwt342" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-80" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-80"}}"><a href="#cite_note-80" id="mwAvs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAvw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv0">[</span>79<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAv4">]</span></span></a></sup> It can detect an extremely broad range of frequencies ranging from 55<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAv8"> </span>Hz to 79<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAwA"> </span>kHz, whereas humans can only detect frequencies between 20<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAwE"> </span>Hz and 20<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwAwI"> </span>kHz. It can hear a range of 10.5 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Octave" title="Octave" id="mwAwM">octaves</a>, compared to about 9 octaves for humans and dogs.<sup about="#mwt345" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-81" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-81"}}"><a href="#cite_note-81" id="mwAwQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwY">[</span>80<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwc">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt348" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-82" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-82"}}"><a href="#cite_note-82" id="mwAwg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAwk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAwo">[</span>81<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAws">]</span></span></a></sup> Its hearing sensitivity is enhanced by its large movable outer ears, the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinna_(anatomy)" title="Pinna (anatomy)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAww">pinnae</a>, which amplify sounds and help detect the location of a noise. It can detect <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ultrasound" title="Ultrasound" id="mwAw0">ultrasound</a>, including ultrasonic calls from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodent" title="Rodent" id="mwAw4">rodent</a> prey.<sup about="#mwt351" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Sunquist_83-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Sunquist"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Sunquist-83"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Sunquist-83" id="mwAw8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAxA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxE">[</span>82<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxI">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt354" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-84" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-84"}}"><a href="#cite_note-84" id="mwAxM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAxQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxU">[</span>83<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxY">]</span></span></a></sup> Research has shown that cats have socio-spatial cognitive abilities to create mental maps of familiar people's locations based on hearing their voices.<sup about="#mwt357" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-85" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-85"}}"><a href="#cite_note-85" id="mwAxc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAxg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxk">[</span>84<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAxo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="17" id="mwAxs" aria-labelledby="Smell"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Smell">Smell</h3></div>
<p id="mwAxw">Cats have an acute sense of smell, due in part to their well-developed <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_bulb" title="Olfactory bulb" id="mwAx0">olfactory bulb</a> and a large surface of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olfactory_mucosa" title="Olfactory mucosa" id="mwAx4">olfactory mucosa</a>, about <span about="#mwt358" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwAx8" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"5.8"},"2":{"wt":"cm2"},"3":{"wt":"in2"},"abbr":{"wt":"on"}},"i":0}}]}">5.8</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt358"> </span><span about="#mwt358">cm</span><sup about="#mwt358">2</sup><span about="#mwt358"> (0.90</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt358"> </span><span about="#mwt358">in</span><sup about="#mwt358">2</sup><span about="#mwt358">)</span> in area, which is about twice that of humans<!-- impossible logic and only 1.7-fold less than the average dog. -->.<sup about="#mwt361" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Moulton_1967_86-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Moulton 1967"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Moulton_1967-86"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Moulton_1967-86" id="mwAyA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAyE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyI">[</span>85<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyM">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats and many other animals have a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobson's_organ" title="Jacobson's organ" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAyQ">Jacobson's organ</a> in their mouths that is used in the behavioral process of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flehmen_response" title="Flehmen response" id="mwAyU">flehmening</a>. It allows them to sense certain aromas in a way that humans cannot. Cats are sensitive to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_pheromone" title="Cat pheromone" id="mwAyY">pheromones</a> such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3-mercapto-3-methylbutan-1-ol" title="3-mercapto-3-methylbutan-1-ol" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAyc">3-mercapto-3-methylbutan-1-ol</a>,<sup about="#mwt364" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-felinine_87-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"felinine"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-felinine-87"}}"><a href="#cite_note-felinine-87" id="mwAyg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAyk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAyo">[</span>86<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAys">]</span></span></a></sup> which they use to communicate through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine_spraying" title="Urine spraying" class="mw-redirect" id="mwAyw">urine spraying</a> and marking with <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent_gland" title="Scent gland" id="mwAy0">scent glands</a>.<sup about="#mwt365" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Sommerville_88-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Sommerville"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Sommerville-88" id="mwAy4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAy8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzA">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzE">]</span></span></a></sup> Many cats also respond strongly to plants that contain <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepetalactone" title="Nepetalactone" id="mwAzI">nepetalactone</a>, especially <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catnip" title="Catnip" id="mwAzM">catnip</a>, which they can detect at less than one part per billion.<sup about="#mwt368" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-89" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-89"}}"><a href="#cite_note-89" id="mwAzQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAzU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzY">[</span>88<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzc">]</span></span></a></sup> About 70–80% of cats are affected by nepetalactone.<sup about="#mwt371" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-90" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-90"}}"><a href="#cite_note-90" id="mwAzg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwAzk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzo">[</span>89<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwAzs">]</span></span></a></sup> This response is also produced by other plants, such as silver vine (<i id="mwAzw"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Actinidia_polygama" title="Actinidia polygama" id="mwAz0">Actinidia polygama</a></i>) and the herb <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerian_(herb)" title="Valerian (herb)" id="mwAz4">valerian</a>; it may be caused by the smell of these plants mimicking a pheromone and stimulating cats' social or sexual behaviors.<sup about="#mwt374" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Tucker_91-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Tucker"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Tucker-91"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Tucker-91" id="mwAz8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA0A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0E">[</span>90<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0I">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="18" id="mwA0M" aria-labelledby="Taste"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Taste">Taste</h3></div>
<p id="mwA0Q">Cats have about 470 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_bud" title="Taste bud" id="mwA0U">taste buds</a>, compared to more than 9,000 on the human tongue.<sup about="#mwt377" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-sch_92-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"sch"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-sch-92"}}"><a href="#cite_note-sch-92" id="mwA0Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA0c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0g">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA0k">]</span></span></a></sup> Domestic and wild cats share a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taste_receptor#Loss_of_function" title="Taste receptor" id="mwA0o">taste receptor gene mutation</a> that keeps their sweet taste buds from binding to sugary molecules, leaving them with no ability to taste <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweetness" title="Sweetness" id="mwA0s">sweetness</a>.<sup about="#mwt380" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-93" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-93"}}"><a href="#cite_note-93" id="mwA0w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA00"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA04">[</span>92<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA08">]</span></span></a></sup> But they do have taste bud receptors specialized for <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acid" title="Acid" id="mwA1A">acids</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amino_acid" title="Amino acid" id="mwA1E">amino acids</a> such as the constituents of protein, and bitter tastes.<sup about="#mwt383" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bradshaw2006_94-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bradshaw2006"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bradshaw2006-94"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bradshaw2006-94" id="mwA1I"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA1M"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1Q">[</span>93<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA1U">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA1Y">Cats' taste buds possess the receptors needed to detect <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umami" title="Umami" id="mwA1c">umami</a>. However, these receptors contain molecular changes that make them taste umami differently from humans. In humans, they detect the amino acids <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glutamic_acid" title="Glutamic acid" id="mwA1g">glutamic acid</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspartic_acid" title="Aspartic acid" id="mwA1k">aspartic acid</a>; but in cats, they instead detect <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inosine_monophosphate" title="Inosine monophosphate" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA1o">inosine monophosphate</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Histidine" title="Histidine" id="mwA1s">histidine</a>.<sup about="#mwt386" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop_95-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"McGrane Gibbs Hernangomez de Alvaro Dunlop"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95"}}"><a href="#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95" id="mwA1w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA10"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA14">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA18">]</span></span></a></sup> These molecules are particularly enriched in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuna" title="Tuna" id="mwA2A">tuna</a>.<sup about="#mwt387" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop_95-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"McGrane Gibbs Hernangomez de Alvaro Dunlop"}}"><a href="#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95" id="mwA2E"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA2I"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2M">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2Q">]</span></span></a></sup> Researchers argue why cats find tuna so <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palatability" title="Palatability" id="mwA2U">palatable</a>: "the specific combination of the high IMP and free histidine contents of tuna, which produces a strong umami taste synergy that is highly preferred by cats."<sup about="#mwt388" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop_95-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"McGrane Gibbs Hernangomez de Alvaro Dunlop"}}"><a href="#cite_note-McGrane_Gibbs_Hernangomez_de_Alvaro_Dunlop-95" id="mwA2Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA2c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2g">[</span>94<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2k">]</span></span></a></sup> One researcher said, "I think umami is as important for cats as sweet is for humans."<sup about="#mwt391" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Science_Tuna_Cat_96-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Science Tuna Cat"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Science_Tuna_Cat-96"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Science_Tuna_Cat-96" id="mwA2o"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA2s"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA2w">[</span>95<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA20">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA24">Cats distinctly prefer food temperature around <span about="#mwt392" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwA28" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"38"},"2":{"wt":"C"},"3":{"wt":"F"},"abbr":{"wt":"on"}},"i":0}}]}">38</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt392"> </span><span about="#mwt392">°C (100</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt392"> </span><span about="#mwt392">°F)</span>, similar to a fresh kill. Some cats reject cold food, which would signal to the cat that the prey is long dead and therefore possibly toxic or decomposing.<sup about="#mwt393" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-sch_92-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"sch"}}"><a href="#cite_note-sch-92" id="mwA3A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA3E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3I">[</span>91<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA3M">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="19" id="mwA3Q" aria-labelledby="Whiskers"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Whiskers">Whiskers</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwA3U"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittyply_edit1.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwA3Y"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittyply_edit1.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Kittyply_edit1.jpg/250px-Kittyply_edit1.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1728" data-file-height="1152" data-file-type="bitmap" height="167" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bb/Kittyply_edit1.jpg/500px-Kittyply_edit1.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwA3c"></a><figcaption id="mwA3g">The whiskers of a cat are highly sensitive to touch.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwA3k">To aid with navigation and sensation, cats have dozens of movable <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vibrissa" title="Vibrissa" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA3o">whiskers (vibrissae)</a> over their body, most prominently on their faces, as seen by the long, white lines diverging outwards from its nose. These provide information on the width of gaps and on the location of objects in the dark, both by touching objects directly and by sensing air currents.
