They trigger protective <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink_reflex" title="Blink reflex" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA3s">blink reflexes</a> to protect the eyes from damage.<sup about="#mwt395" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Case_59-3" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Case"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Case-59" id="mwA3w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA30"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA34">[</span>58<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA38">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt394" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwA4A" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"47"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 47"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>47<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup></p>

</section></section><section data-mw-section-id="20" id="mwA4E" aria-labelledby="Behavior"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Behavior">Behavior</h2></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt396" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwA4I" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"See also","href":"./Template:See_also"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat behavior"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt397" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt396" id="mwA4M">See also: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_behavior" title="Cat behavior">Cat behavior</a></div>
<p id="mwA4Q">Outdoor cats are active both day and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nocturnal_animal" title="Nocturnal animal" id="mwA4U">night</a>, although they tend to be slightly more active at night.<sup about="#mwt401" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-97" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-97"}}"><a href="#cite_note-97" id="mwA4Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA4c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4g">[</span>96<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA4k">]</span></span></a></sup> Domestic cats spend the majority of their time in the vicinity of their homes, but they can range a radius of many hundreds of meters. They establish <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territory_(animal)" title="Territory (animal)" id="mwA4o">territories</a> that vary considerably in size, in one study ranging <span about="#mwt398" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwA4s" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"7"},"2":{"wt":"-"},"3":{"wt":"28"},"4":{"wt":"ha"},"5":{"wt":"acre"}},"i":0}}]}">7–28</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt398"> </span><span about="#mwt398">ha (17–69 acres)</span>.<sup about="#mwt404" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-98" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-98"}}"><a href="#cite_note-98" id="mwA4w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA40"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA44">[</span>97<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA48">]</span></span></a></sup> The timing of cats' activity is quite flexible and varied; but being low-light predators, they are generally <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crepuscular_animal" title="Crepuscular animal" id="mwA5A">crepuscular</a>, which means they tend to be more active near dawn and dusk. However, house cats' behavior is also influenced by human activity, and they may adapt to their owners' sleeping patterns to some extent.<sup about="#mwt407" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-99" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-99"}}"><a href="#cite_note-99" id="mwA5E"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA5I"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5M">[</span>98<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5Q">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt410" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-100" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-100"}}"><a href="#cite_note-100" id="mwA5U"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA5Y"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5c">[</span>99<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA5g">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA5k">Cats conserve energy by sleeping more than most animals, especially as they grow older. The daily duration of sleep varies, usually between 12 and 16 hours, with 13 to 14 being the average. Some cats can sleep as much as 20 hours. The term "cat nap" for a short rest refers to the cat's tendency to fall asleep (lightly) for a brief period. Short periods of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_eye_movement_sleep" title="Rapid eye movement sleep" id="mwA5o">rapid eye movement sleep</a> are often accompanied by muscle twitches, which suggests they are dreaming.<sup about="#mwt413" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-101" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-101"}}"><a href="#cite_note-101" id="mwA5s"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA5w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA50">[</span>100<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA54">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA58">Behavioral and personality traits depend on a complex interplay between genetic and environmental factors. Scientific evidence does not support the popular belief that those traits are linked to coat colors.<sup about="#mwt416" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-102" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-102"}}"><a href="#cite_note-102" id="mwA6A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA6E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6I">[</span>101<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6M">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt419" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-103" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-103"}}"><a href="#cite_note-103" id="mwA6Q"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA6U"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6Y">[</span>102<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6c">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt422" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-104" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-104"}}"><a href="#cite_note-104" id="mwA6g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA6k"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6o">[</span>103<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA6s">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<section data-mw-section-id="21" id="mwA6w" aria-labelledby="Sociability"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Sociability">Sociability</h3></div>
<p id="mwA60">The social behavior of the domestic cat ranges from widely dispersed individuals to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feral_cat_colony" title="Feral cat colony" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA64">feral cat colonies</a> that gather around a food source, based on groups of co-operating females.<sup about="#mwt425" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Crowell-davis2004_105-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Crowell-davis2004"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Crowell-davis2004-105"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Crowell-davis2004-105" id="mwA68"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA7A"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7E">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7I">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt428" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Liberg_al2014_106-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Liberg_al2014"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Liberg_al2014-106"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Liberg_al2014-106" id="mwA7M"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA7Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7U">[</span>105<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7Y">]</span></span></a></sup> Within such groups, one cat is usually dominant over the others.<sup about="#mwt431" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-107" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-107"}}"><a href="#cite_note-107" id="mwA7c"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA7g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7k">[</span>106<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA7o">]</span></span></a></sup> Each cat in a colony holds a distinct territory, with sexually active males having the largest territories, which are about 10 times larger than those of female cats and may overlap with several females' territories. These territories are marked by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine_spraying" title="Urine spraying" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA7s">urine spraying</a>, rubbing objects at head height with secretions from facial glands, and by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecation" title="Defecation" id="mwA7w">defecation</a>.<sup about="#mwt434" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Sommerville_88-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Sommerville"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Sommerville-88"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Sommerville-88" id="mwA70"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA74"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA78">[</span>87<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA8A">]</span></span></a></sup> Between these territories are neutral areas where cats watch and greet one another without territorial conflicts. Outside these neutral areas, territory holders usually chase away stranger cats, at first by staring, hissing, and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growling" title="Growling" id="mwA8E">growling</a>, and, if that does not work, by short and violent, noisy attacks. Because cats do not have a social survival strategy or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herd_behavior" title="Herd behavior" id="mwA8I">herd behavior</a>, they always hunt alone.<sup about="#mwt437" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bradshaw_108-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bradshaw"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bradshaw-108"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bradshaw-108" id="mwA8M"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA8Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA8U">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA8Y">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwA8c"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwA8g"><img alt="Two kittens resting side by side, an instinctive behavior that offers both protection and comfort" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg/250px-Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="3922" data-file-height="2204" data-file-type="bitmap" height="140" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg/500px-Kittens_resting_close_together_for_warmth_and_security.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwA8k"></a><figcaption id="mwA8o">Two kittens lying side by side, an instinctive behavior that offers both comfort and protection</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwA8s">Life in proximity to humans and other domestic animals has led to a symbiotic social adaptation in cats, and cats may express great affection toward humans or other animals. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethology" title="Ethology" id="mwA8w">Ethologically</a>, a cat's human keeper functions as a mother surrogate.<sup about="#mwt440" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-109" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-109"}}"><a href="#cite_note-109" id="mwA80"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA84"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA88">[</span>108<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA9A">]</span></span></a></sup> Adult cats live in a type of extended kittenhood, a form of behavioral <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoteny" title="Neoteny" id="mwA9E">neoteny</a>. Their high-pitched sounds may mimic the cries of a hungry human infant, making them particularly difficult for humans to ignore.<sup about="#mwt443" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-McComb_2009_110-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"McComb 2009"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-McComb_2009-110"}}"><a href="#cite_note-McComb_2009-110" id="mwA9I"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA9M"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA9Q">[</span>109<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA9U">]</span></span></a></sup> Some pet cats are poorly socialized. In particular, older cats may show aggressiveness toward newly arrived kittens, which includes biting and scratching; this type of behavior is known as feline asocial aggression.<sup about="#mwt446" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Levine_2005_111-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Levine 2005"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Levine_2005-111"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Levine_2005-111" id="mwA9Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA9c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA9g">[</span>110<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA9k">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA9o"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redirected_aggression" title="Redirected aggression" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA9s">Redirected aggression</a> is a common form of aggression that can occur in multiple cat households. In redirected aggression, a cat is usually agitated by a stimulus such as a sight, sound, or other trigger that causes heightened anxiety or arousal; if the cat cannot attack the original stimulus, it may redirect its aggression toward the nearest cat, pet, human, or other being.<sup about="#mwt449" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Horwitz_112-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Horwitz"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Horwitz-112"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Horwitz-112" id="mwA9w"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA90"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA94">[</span>111<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA98">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt452" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Behaviorist_113-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Behaviorist"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Behaviorist-113"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Behaviorist-113" id="mwA-A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA-E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-I">[</span>112<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-M">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwA-Q">Domestic cats' <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scent_rubbing" title="Scent rubbing" id="mwA-U">scent rubbing</a> behavior toward humans or other cats is thought to be a feline means of social bonding.<sup about="#mwt455" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-114" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-114"}}"><a href="#cite_note-114" id="mwA-Y"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA-c"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-g">[</span>113<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA-k">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<div class="listen-file-header"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meow_domestic_cat.ogg" title="File:Meow domestic cat.ogg">A meow</a></div>
<div><span typeof="mw:File" class="mw-default-audio-height"><span><span class="mw-tmh-player audio mw-file-element" style="width: 215px;"><audio preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" height="32" width="215" style="width: 215px;" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meow_domestic_cat.ogg" data-durationhint="2" class="" playsinline="" id="undefined_placeholder" disabled="disabled" tabindex="-1"></audio><a class="mw-tmh-play" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Meow_domestic_cat.ogg" title="Play audio" role="button"><span class="mw-tmh-play-icon notheme"></span></a><span class="mw-tmh-duration mw-tmh-label"><span class="sr-only">Duration: 2 seconds.</span><span aria-hidden="true">0:02</span></span></span></span></span></div>
<div class="description"></div></div></div></div>
</div><span class="mw-empty-elt"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_with_hAudio_microformats"><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Listen_template_using_plain_parameter"></span></td></tr></tbody></table>
<p id="mwA-8">Domestic cats use many <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_communication" title="Animal communication" id="mwA_A">vocalizations</a> for communication, including <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purr" title="Purr" id="mwA_E">purring</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trill_consonant" title="Trill consonant" id="mwA_I">trilling</a>, hissing, growling/snarling, grunting, and several different forms of meowing.<sup about="#mwt466" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Moelk1944_115-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Moelk1944"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Moelk1944-115"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Moelk1944-115" id="mwA_M"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA_Q"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA_U">[</span>114<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA_Y">]</span></span></a></sup> Their <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_body_language" title="Cat body language" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_c">body language</a>, including position of ears and tail, relaxation of the whole body, and kneading of the paws, are all indicators of mood. The tail and ears are particularly important social signal mechanisms; a raised tail indicates a friendly greeting, and flattened ears indicate hostility. Tail-raising also indicates the cat's position in the group's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_hierarchy" title="Social hierarchy" class="mw-redirect" id="mwA_g">social hierarchy</a>, with dominant individuals raising their tails less often than subordinate ones.<sup about="#mwt469" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-116" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-116"}}"><a href="#cite_note-116" id="mwA_k"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA_o"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA_s">[</span>115<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA_w">]</span></span></a></sup> Feral cats are generally silent.<sup about="#mwt472" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Jensen_117-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Jensen"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Jensen-117"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Jensen-117" id="mwA_0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwA_4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwA_8">[</span>116<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt463" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBAE" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"208"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 208"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>208<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> Nose-to-nose touching is also a common greeting and may be followed by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_grooming" title="Social grooming" id="mwBAI">social grooming</a>, which is solicited by one of the cats raising and tilting its head.<sup about="#mwt473" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Crowell-davis2004_105-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Crowell-davis2004"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Crowell-davis2004-105" id="mwBAM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBAQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAU">[</span>104<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBAc"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purring" title="Purring" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBAg">Purring</a> may have developed as an evolutionary advantage as a signaling mechanism of reassurance between mother cats and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breastfeeding" title="Breastfeeding" id="mwBAk">nursing</a> kittens, who are thought to use it as a care-soliciting signal.<sup about="#mwt474" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-bradshaw2012_118-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"bradshaw2012"}}"><a href="#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118" id="mwBAo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBAs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBAw">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBA0">]</span></span></a></sup> Post-nursing cats also often purr as a sign of contentment: when being petted, becoming relaxed,<sup about="#mwt477" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-BruelKjaer_119-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"BruelKjaer"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-BruelKjaer-119"}}"><a href="#cite_note-BruelKjaer-119" id="mwBA4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBA8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBA">[</span>118<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBE">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt480" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-IsnareCom_120-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"IsnareCom"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-IsnareCom-120"}}"><a href="#cite_note-IsnareCom-120" id="mwBBI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBQ">[</span>119<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBU">]</span></span></a></sup> or eating. Although purring is popularly interpreted as indicative of pleasure, it has been recorded in a wide variety of circumstances, most of which involve physical contact between the cat and another, presumably trusted individual.<sup about="#mwt481" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-bradshaw2012_118-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"bradshaw2012"}}"><a href="#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118" id="mwBBY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBg">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBk">]</span></span></a></sup> Some cats have been observed to purr continuously when chronically ill or in apparent pain.<sup about="#mwt484" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-121" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-121"}}"><a href="#cite_note-121" id="mwBBo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBBs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBBw">[</span>120<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBB0">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBB4">The exact mechanism by which cats purr has long been elusive, but it has been proposed that purring is generated via a series of sudden build-ups and releases of pressure as the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glottis" title="Glottis" id="mwBB8">glottis</a> is opened and closed, which causes the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vocal_folds" title="Vocal folds" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBCA">vocal folds</a> to separate forcefully. The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larynx" title="Larynx" id="mwBCE">laryngeal muscles</a> in control of the glottis are thought to be driven by a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_oscillation" title="Neural oscillation" id="mwBCI">neural oscillator</a> which generates a cycle of contraction and release every 30–40 <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millisecond" title="Millisecond" id="mwBCM">milliseconds</a> (giving a frequency of 33 to 25 Hz).<sup about="#mwt487" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-bradshaw2012_118-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"bradshaw2012"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-bradshaw2012-118"}}"><a href="#cite_note-bradshaw2012-118" id="mwBCQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBCU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCY">[</span>117<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCc">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt490" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-122" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-122"}}"><a href="#cite_note-122" id="mwBCg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBCk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCo">[</span>121<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBCs">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt493" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-123" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-123"}}"><a href="#cite_note-123" id="mwBCw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBC0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBC4">[</span>122<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBC8">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBDA">Domestic cats observed in rescue facilities have 276 morphologically distinct <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_expression" title="Facial expression" id="mwBDE">facial expressions</a> based on 26 facial movements; each facial expression corresponds to different social functions that are probably influenced by domestication.<sup about="#mwt496" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-124" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-124"}}"><a href="#cite_note-124" id="mwBDI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBDM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDQ">[</span>123<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDU">]</span></span></a></sup> Facial expressions have helped researchers detect pain in cats. The feline <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimace_scale" title="Grimace scale" id="mwBDY">grimace scale</a>'s five criteria—ear position, orbital tightening, muzzle tension, whisker change, and head position—indicated the presence of acute pain in cats.<sup about="#mwt499" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-125" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-125"}}"><a href="#cite_note-125" id="mwBDc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBDg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDk">[</span>124<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBDo">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt502" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-126" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-126"}}"><a href="#cite_note-126" id="mwBDs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBDw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBD0">[</span>125<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBD4">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="23" id="mwBD8" aria-labelledby="Grooming"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Grooming">Grooming</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-left" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBEA"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_tongue_macro.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBEE"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_tongue_macro.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Cat_tongue_macro.jpg/250px-Cat_tongue_macro.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="800" data-file-height="528" data-file-type="bitmap" height="119" width="180" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Cat_tongue_macro.jpg/500px-Cat_tongue_macro.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.7" id="mwBEI"></a><figcaption id="mwBEM">Cat tongue</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBEQ">Cats are known for spending considerable amounts of time licking their coats to keep them clean.<sup about="#mwt504" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-hairballs_127-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"hairballs"}}"><a href="#cite_note-hairballs-127" id="mwBEU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBEY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEc">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt507" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-128" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-128"}}"><a href="#cite_note-128" id="mwBEk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBEo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEs">[</span>127<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBEw">]</span></span></a></sup> The cat's tongue has backward-facing spines about 0.5 millimeter long, called <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filiform_papillae" title="Filiform papillae" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBE0">filiform papillae</a>, which contain <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keratin" title="Keratin" id="mwBE4">keratin</a> making them rigid.<sup about="#mwt510" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Boshel_1982_129-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Boshel 1982"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Boshel_1982-129"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Boshel_1982-129" id="mwBE8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBFA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBFE">[</span>128<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBFI">]</span></span></a></sup> The papillae act like a hairbrush, and some cats, particularly <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_long-haired_cat" title="Domestic long-haired cat" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBFM">long-haired cats</a>, occasionally regurgitate sausage-shaped <span about="#mwt503" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBFQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"cvt","href":"./Template:Cvt"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"2"},"2":{"wt":"–"},"3":{"wt":"3"},"4":{"wt":"cm"},"5":{"wt":"1"}},"i":0}}]}">2–3</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt503"> </span><span about="#mwt503">cm (0.8–1.2</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt503"> </span><span about="#mwt503">in)</span> long <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hairball" title="Hairball" id="mwBFU">hairballs</a> of fur that have collected in their stomachs from grooming. Hairballs can be prevented with remedies that ease elimination of the hair through the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gut_(anatomy)" title="Gut (anatomy)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBFY">gut</a>, and regular grooming of the coat with a comb or stiff brush.<sup about="#mwt513" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-hairballs_127-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"hairballs"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-hairballs-127"}}"><a href="#cite_note-hairballs-127" id="mwBFc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBFg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBFk">[</span>126<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBFo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="24" id="mwBFs" aria-labelledby="Cat_intelligence"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Cat_intelligence">Cat intelligence</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt514" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBFw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat intelligence"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt515" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt514" id="mwBF0">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_intelligence" title="Cat intelligence">Cat intelligence</a></div>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBF4"><span id="mwBF8"><span class="mw-tmh-player video"><video poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Cat_opening_door.webm/250px--Cat_opening_door.webm.jpg" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" height="444" width="250" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_opening_door.webm" data-durationhint="23" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBGA_placeholder" playsinline="" disabled="disabled" tabindex="-1" style="aspect-ratio: 250 / 444;"></video><a class="mw-tmh-play" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_opening_door.webm" title="Play video" role="button"><span class="mw-tmh-play-icon notheme"></span></a><span class="mw-tmh-duration mw-tmh-label"><span class="sr-only">Duration: 23 seconds.</span><span aria-hidden="true">0:23</span></span></span></span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cat_opening_door.webm" class="mw-file-magnify"></a><figcaption id="mwBGQ">A cat uses problem-solving skills to open a door.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBGU">Cat intelligence refers to a cat's ability to solve problems, adapt to its environment, learn new behaviors, and communicate its needs. Structurally, a cat's brain shares similarities with the human brain,<sup about="#mwt519" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Gross_20102_130-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Gross 20102"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Gross_20102-130"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Gross_20102-130" id="mwBGY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBGc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGg">[</span>129<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGk">]</span></span></a></sup> containing around 250 million neurons in the cerebral cortex, which is responsible for complex processing.<sup about="#mwt522" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-131" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-131"}}"><a href="#cite_note-131" id="mwBGo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBGs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBGw">[</span>130<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBG0">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats display <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuroplasticity" title="Neuroplasticity" id="mwBG4">neuroplasticity</a> allowing their brains to reorganize based on experiences. They have well-developed memory retaining information for a decade or longer. These memories are often intertwined with emotions, allowing cats to recall both positive and negative experiences associated with specific places.<sup about="#mwt525" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-132" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-132"}}"><a href="#cite_note-132" id="mwBG8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBHA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHE">[</span>131<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHI">]</span></span></a></sup> While they excel in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observational_learning" title="Observational learning" id="mwBHM">observational learning</a> and problem-solving, studies conclude that they struggle with understanding cause-and-effect relationships in the same way that humans do.<sup about="#mwt528" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-133" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-133"}}"><a href="#cite_note-133" id="mwBHQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBHU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHY">[</span>132<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBHg">Cat <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_cognition" title="Animal cognition" id="mwBHk">intelligence</a> study is mostly from consideration of the domesticated cat. Living in urban environments has exposed it to challenges that require adaptive behaviors, contributing to cognitive development.<sup about="#mwt531" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-134" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-134"}}"><a href="#cite_note-134" id="mwBHo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBHs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBHw">[</span>133<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBH0">]</span></span></a></sup> Selective breeding and genetic changes have further influenced its intelligence.<sup about="#mwt532" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007_38-2" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007"}}"><a href="#cite_note-DriscollMenotti-Raymond2007-38" id="mwBH4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBH8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIA">[</span>37<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIE">]</span></span></a></sup> Kittens learn essential survival skills by observing their mothers, while adult cats refine their abilities through <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_and_error" title="Trial and error" id="mwBII">trial and error</a>.<sup about="#mwt535" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-135" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-135"}}"><a href="#cite_note-135" id="mwBIM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBIQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIU">[</span>134<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBIY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="25" id="mwBIc" aria-labelledby="Play"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Play">Play</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt536" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBIg" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Main","href":"./Template:Main"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat play and toys"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt537" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt536" id="mwBIk">Main article: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_play_and_toys" title="Cat play and toys">Cat play and toys</a></div>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBIo" data-mw="{"attribs":[["thumbtime",{"txt":"4"}],["alt",{"txt":"Play fight between kittens, age 14 weeks"}]]}"><span id="mwBIs"><span class="mw-tmh-player video"><video poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm/250px-seek%3D4-Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm.jpg" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" height="141" width="250" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm" data-durationhint="295" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBIw_placeholder" playsinline="" disabled="disabled" tabindex="-1" style="aspect-ratio: 250 / 141;"></video><a class="mw-tmh-play" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm" title="Play video" role="button"><span class="mw-tmh-play-icon notheme"></span></a></span></span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Play_fight_between_cats.webmhd.webm" class="mw-file-magnify"></a><figcaption id="mwBJA">Kittens aged 14 weeks use fighting as a form of play.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBJE">Domestic cats, especially young kittens, are known for their love of play. This behavior mimics hunting and is important in helping kittens learn to stalk, capture, and kill prey.<sup about="#mwt540" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-136" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-136"}}"><a href="#cite_note-136" id="mwBJI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJQ">[</span>135<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJU">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats also engage in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough-and-tumble_play" title="Rough-and-tumble play" id="mwBJY">play fighting</a>, both with each other and with humans. This behavior may be a way for cats to practice the skills needed for real combat, and it might also reduce the fear that they associate with launching attacks on other animals.<sup about="#mwt543" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-137" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-137"}}"><a href="#cite_note-137" id="mwBJc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJk">[</span>136<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBJs">Cats also tend to play with toys more when they are hungry.<sup about="#mwt546" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-138" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-138"}}"><a href="#cite_note-138" id="mwBJw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBJ0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJ4">[</span>137<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBJ8">]</span></span></a></sup> Owing to the close similarity between play and hunting, cats prefer to play with objects that resemble prey, such as small furry toys that move rapidly, but rapidly lose interest. They become <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habituation" title="Habituation" id="mwBKA">habituated</a> to a toy they have played with before.<sup about="#mwt549" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-139" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-139"}}"><a href="#cite_note-139" id="mwBKE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBKI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKM">[</span>138<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKQ">]</span></span></a></sup> String is often used as a toy, but if it is eaten, it can become caught at the base of the cat's tongue and then move into the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intestine" title="Intestine" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBKU">intestines</a>, a medical emergency which can cause serious illness, even death.<sup about="#mwt552" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-140" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-140"}}"><a href="#cite_note-140" id="mwBKY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBKc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKg">[</span>139<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBKk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="26" id="mwBKo" aria-labelledby="Hunting_and_feeding"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Hunting_and_feeding">Hunting and feeding</h3></div>
<span class="mw-empty-elt" about="#mwt553" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBKs" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"See also","href":"./Template:See_also"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"Cat food"}},"i":0}}]}"><link rel="mw-deduplicated-inline-style" href="mw-data:TemplateStyles:r1353705441" about="#mwt554" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Module:Hatnote/styles.css"},"body":{"extsrc":""}}"></span><div role="note" class="hatnote navigation-not-searchable" about="#mwt553" id="mwBKw">See also: <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_food" title="Cat food">Cat food</a></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBK0"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kot_z_myszą.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBK4"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kot_z_myszą.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Kot_z_mysz%C4%85.jpg/250px-Kot_z_mysz%C4%85.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="2171" data-file-height="2169" data-file-type="bitmap" height="250" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/97/Kot_z_mysz%C4%85.jpg/500px-Kot_z_mysz%C4%85.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBK8"></a><figcaption id="mwBLA">A <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deermouse" title="Deermouse" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBLE">deermouse</a> is the prey of this domestic cat.</figcaption></figure>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBLI"><span id="mwBLM"><span class="mw-tmh-player video"><video poster="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/26/Katt_%C3%A4ter_P%C3%A5f%C3%A5gel%C3%B6ga_2011.webm/250px--Katt_%C3%A4ter_P%C3%A5f%C3%A5gel%C3%B6ga_2011.webm.jpg" preload="none" data-mw-tmh="" height="157" width="250" resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Katt_äter_Påfågelöga_2011.webm" data-durationhint="62" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBLQ_placeholder" playsinline="" disabled="disabled" tabindex="-1" style="aspect-ratio: 250 / 157;"></video><a class="mw-tmh-play" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Katt_äter_Påfågelöga_2011.webm" title="Play video" role="button"><span class="mw-tmh-play-icon notheme"></span></a><span class="mw-tmh-duration mw-tmh-label"><span class="sr-only">Duration: 1 minute and 2 seconds.</span><span aria-hidden="true">1:02</span></span></span></span><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Katt_äter_Påfågelöga_2011.webm" class="mw-file-magnify"></a><figcaption id="mwBLc">A domestic cat caught a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aglais_io" title="Aglais io" id="mwBLg">peacock butterfly</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBLk">The shape and structure of cats' cheeks is insufficient to allow them to take in liquids using suction. Lapping at a rate of four times a second, the cat touches the smooth tip of its tongue to the surface of the water, and quickly retracts it like a corkscrew, drawing water upward into their mouths.<sup about="#mwt557" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Reis_2010_141-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Reis 2010"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Reis_2010-141"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Reis_2010-141" id="mwBLo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBLs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBLw">[</span>140<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBL0">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt560" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Kim_2012_142-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Kim 2012"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Kim_2012-142"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Kim_2012-142" id="mwBL4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBL8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMA">[</span>141<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBME">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBMI">Feral cats and free-fed house cats consume several small meals in a day. The frequency and size of meals varies between individuals. They select food based on its temperature, smell, and texture; they dislike chilled foods and respond most strongly to moist foods rich in amino acids, which are similar to meat. Cats reject novel flavors (a response termed <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neophobia" title="Neophobia" id="mwBMM">neophobia</a>) and learn quickly to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conditioned_taste_aversion" title="Conditioned taste aversion" id="mwBMQ">avoid foods that have tasted unpleasant</a> in the past.<sup about="#mwt561" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bradshaw_108-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bradshaw"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bradshaw-108" id="mwBMU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBMY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMc">[</span>107<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt564" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Zaghini_143-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Zaghini"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Zaghini-143"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Zaghini-143" id="mwBMk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBMo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMs">[</span>142<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBMw">]</span></span></a></sup> It is also a common misconception that all cats like milk or cream, as they tend to avoid sweet food and milk. Most adult cats are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lactose_intolerant" title="Lactose intolerant" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBM0">lactose intolerant</a>; the sugar in milk is not easily digested and may cause soft stools or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diarrhea" title="Diarrhea" id="mwBM4">diarrhea</a>.<sup about="#mwt567" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Kienzle_1994_144-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Kienzle 1994"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Kienzle_1994-144"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Kienzle_1994-144" id="mwBM8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBNA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNE">[</span>143<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNI">]</span></span></a></sup> Some also develop odd eating habits and like to eat or chew on things such as wool, plastic, cables, paper, string, aluminum foil, or even coal. This condition, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pica_(disorder)" title="Pica (disorder)" id="mwBNM">pica</a>, can threaten their health, depending on the amount and toxicity of the items eaten.<sup about="#mwt570" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bradshaw_1997_145-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bradshaw 1997"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bradshaw_1997-145"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bradshaw_1997-145" id="mwBNQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBNU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNY">[</span>144<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNc">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBNg">Cats hunt small prey, primarily birds and rodents,<sup about="#mwt574" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Woods_146-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Woods"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Woods-146"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Woods-146" id="mwBNk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBNo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNs">[</span>145<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBNw">]</span></span></a></sup> and are often used as a form of pest control.<sup about="#mwt577" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-147" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-147"}}"><a href="#cite_note-147" id="mwBN0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBN4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBN8">[</span>146<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOA">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt580" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-148" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-148"}}"><a href="#cite_note-148" id="mwBOE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBOI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOM">[</span>147<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Other common small creatures, such as lizards, snakes and insects, may also become prey.<sup about="#mwt583" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-149" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-149"}}"><a href="#cite_note-149" id="mwBOU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBOY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOc">[</span>148<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOg">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt586" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-150" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-150"}}"><a href="#cite_note-150" id="mwBOk"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBOo"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOs">[</span>149<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBOw">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats use two hunting strategies, either stalking prey actively, or <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ambush_predator" title="Ambush predator" id="mwBO0">waiting in ambush</a> until a prey animal comes close enough to be captured.<sup about="#mwt589" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-How_Cats_Evolved_to_Win_the_Internet_151-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"How Cats Evolved to Win the Internet"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-How_Cats_Evolved_to_Win_the_Internet-151"}}"><a href="#cite_note-How_Cats_Evolved_to_Win_the_Internet-151" id="mwBO4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBO8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPA">[</span>150<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPE">]</span></span></a></sup> The strategy used depends on available prey, with cats waiting in ambush outside burrows, but tending to actively stalk birds.<sup about="#mwt592" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Turner_2000_152-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Turner 2000"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Turner_2000-152"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Turner_2000-152" id="mwBPI"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBPM"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPQ">[</span>151<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPU">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt571" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBPY" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"153"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 153"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>153<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup> Domestic cats are a major <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_predation_on_wildlife" title="Cat predation on wildlife" id="mwBPc">predators of wildlife</a> in the United States, killing an estimated 1.3 to 4.0<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwBPg"> </span>billion birds and 6.3 to 22.3<span typeof="mw:Entity" id="mwBPk"> </span>billion mammals annually.<sup about="#mwt595" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-NC012913_153-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"NC012913"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-NC012913-153"}}"><a href="#cite_note-NC012913-153" id="mwBPo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBPs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBPw">[</span>152<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBP0">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBP4">Certain species appear more susceptible than others; in one English village, for example, 30% of house sparrow mortality was linked to the domestic cat.<sup about="#mwt598" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Chucher_1987_154-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Chucher 1987"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Chucher_1987-154"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Chucher_1987-154" id="mwBP8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQE">[</span>153<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQI">]</span></span></a></sup> In the recovery of ringed robins (<i id="mwBQM"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erithacus_rubecula" title="Erithacus rubecula" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBQQ">Erithacus rubecula</a></i>) and dunnocks (<i id="mwBQU"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prunella_modularis" title="Prunella modularis" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBQY">Prunella modularis</a></i>) in Britain, 31% of deaths were a result of cat predation.<sup about="#mwt601" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Mead_1982_183–186_155-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Mead 1982 183–186"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Mead_1982_183–186-155"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Mead_1982_183–186-155" id="mwBQc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQk">[</span>154<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBQo">]</span></span></a></sup> In parts of North America, the presence of larger carnivores such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote" title="Coyote" id="mwBQs">coyotes</a>, which prey on cats and other small predators, reduces the effect of predation by cats and other small predators such as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opossum" title="Opossum" id="mwBQw">opossums</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raccoon" title="Raccoon" id="mwBQ0">raccoons</a> on bird numbers and variety.<sup about="#mwt604" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Crooks_1999_156-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Crooks 1999"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Crooks_1999-156"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Crooks_1999-156" id="mwBQ4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBQ8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRA">[</span>155<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRE">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBRI">Another poorly understood element of cat hunting behavior is the presentation of prey to human guardians. One explanation is that cats adopt humans into their social group and share excess kill with others in the group according to the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominance_hierarchy" title="Dominance hierarchy" id="mwBRM">dominance hierarchy</a>, in which humans are reacted to as if they are at or near the top.<sup about="#mwt608" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Leyhausen_1978_157-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Leyhausen 1978"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Leyhausen_1978-157"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Leyhausen_1978-157" id="mwBRQ"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBRU"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRY">[</span>156<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRc">]</span></span></a></sup> Another explanation is that they attempt to teach their guardians to hunt or to help their human as if feeding "an elderly cat, or an inept kitten".<sup about="#mwt611" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Morris_Catwatching_1_158-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Morris Catwatching 1"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Morris_Catwatching_1-158"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Morris_Catwatching_1-158" id="mwBRg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBRk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRo">[</span>157<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBRs">]</span></span></a></sup> This hypothesis is inconsistent with the fact that male cats also bring home prey, though males have negligible involvement in raising kittens.<sup about="#mwt612" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Turner_2000_152-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Turner 2000"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Turner_2000-152" id="mwBRw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBR0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBR4">[</span>151<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBR8">]</span></span></a></sup><sup class="reference nowrap" about="#mwt605" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBSA" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"rp","href":"./Template:Rp"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"153"}},"i":0}}]}"><span title="Page / location: 153"><span typeof="mw:Entity">:</span><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span>153<span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="27" id="mwBSE" aria-labelledby="Fighting"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Fighting">Fighting</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBSI"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GAto.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBSM"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GAto.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Gato_enervado_pola_presencia_dun_can.jpg/250px-Gato_enervado_pola_presencia_dun_can.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1200" data-file-height="935" data-file-type="bitmap" height="195" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Gato_enervado_pola_presencia_dun_can.jpg/500px-Gato_enervado_pola_presencia_dun_can.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBSQ"></a><figcaption id="mwBSU">A domestic cat exhibiting a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deimatic_behaviour" title="Deimatic behaviour" id="mwBSY">threat display</a>, hissing and arching its back.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBSc">Domestic males are more likely to fight than females.<sup about="#mwt615" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Lindell_159-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Lindell"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Lindell-159"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Lindell-159" id="mwBSg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBSk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBSo">[</span>158<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBSs">]</span></span></a></sup> The most common reason for feral <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catfight_(animal_behavior)" title="Catfight (animal behavior)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBSw">cat fighting</a> is competition between two males to mate with a female, and most fights are won by the heavier male.<sup about="#mwt618" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-courtship_160-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"courtship"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-courtship-160"}}"><a href="#cite_note-courtship-160" id="mwBS0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBS4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBS8">[</span>159<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTA">]</span></span></a></sup> Another common reason for fighting in domestic cats is the difficulty of establishing territories within a small home.<sup about="#mwt619" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Lindell_159-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Lindell"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Lindell-159" id="mwBTE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBTI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTM">[</span>158<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTQ">]</span></span></a></sup> Female cats also fight over territory or to defend their kittens. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neutering" title="Neutering" id="mwBTU">Neutering</a> decreases or eliminates this behavior in many cases, suggesting that the behavior is linked to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sex_hormone" title="Sex hormone" id="mwBTY">sex hormones</a>.<sup about="#mwt622" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-161" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-161"}}"><a href="#cite_note-161" id="mwBTc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBTg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTk">[</span>160<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBTo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBTs">When cats become aggressive, they try to appear larger and more threatening by raising their fur, arching their backs, turning sideways, hissing, or spitting.<sup about="#mwt625" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-behaviourguide_162-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"behaviourguide"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-behaviourguide-162"}}"><a href="#cite_note-behaviourguide-162" id="mwBTw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBT0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBT4">[</span>161<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBT8">]</span></span></a></sup> Often, the ears are pointed down and back to avoid damage to the inner ear and potentially listen for any changes behind them while focused forward. Cats may also vocalize loudly and bare their teeth in an effort to further intimidate their opponents. Fights usually consist of grappling, slapping the face and body with the forepaws, and bites. Cats throw themselves to the ground in a defensive posture to rake their opponent's belly with their hind legs.<sup about="#mwt628" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-163" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-163"}}"><a href="#cite_note-163" id="mwBUA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBUE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUI">[</span>162<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBUQ">Serious damage is rare, because the fights are usually short, with the loser fleeing with scratches to the face and ears. More severe fights for mating rights may give deep punctures and lacerations. Normally, serious injuries from fighting are limited to infections from scratches and bites. Bites are probably the main route of transmission of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feline_immunodeficiency_virus" title="Feline immunodeficiency virus" id="mwBUU">feline immunodeficiency virus</a>.<sup about="#mwt631" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Pederson_1989_164-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Pederson 1989"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Pederson_1989-164"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Pederson_1989-164" id="mwBUY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBUc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUg">[</span>163<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUk">]</span></span></a></sup> Sexually active males are usually involved in many fights and have battered faces.<sup about="#mwt634" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-165" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-165"}}"><a href="#cite_note-165" id="mwBUo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBUs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBUw">[</span>164<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBU0">]</span></span></a></sup> Cats often threaten animals larger than them to defend their territory, such as dogs and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_fox" title="Red fox" id="mwBU4">foxes</a>.<sup about="#mwt637" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-166" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-166"}}"><a href="#cite_note-166" id="mwBU8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBVA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVE">[</span>165<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBVI">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

</section><section data-mw-section-id="28" id="mwBVM" aria-labelledby="Reproduction"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Reproduction">Reproduction</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBVQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mating_Cats_(Domestic_cats)_in_Kannur.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBVU"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mating_Cats_(Domestic_cats)_in_Kannur.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Mating_Cats_%28Domestic_cats%29_in_Kannur.jpg/250px-Mating_Cats_%28Domestic_cats%29_in_Kannur.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="5568" data-file-height="3712" data-file-type="bitmap" height="167" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Mating_Cats_%28Domestic_cats%29_in_Kannur.jpg/500px-Mating_Cats_%28Domestic_cats%29_in_Kannur.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBVY"></a><figcaption id="mwBVc">When cats mate, the tomcat (male) bites the scruff of the female's neck as she assumes a position conducive to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mating" title="Mating" id="mwBVg">mating</a> known as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lordosis_behavior" title="Lordosis behavior" id="mwBVk">lordosis behavior</a>.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBVo">The cat secretes and perceives <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pheromone" title="Pheromone" id="mwBVs">pheromones</a>.<sup about="#mwt640" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Bland1979_167-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Bland1979"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Bland1979-167"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Bland1979-167" id="mwBVw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBV0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBV4">[</span>166<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBV8">]</span></span></a></sup> Female cats, called <i id="mwBWA">queens</i>, are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polyestrous" title="Polyestrous" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBWE">polyestrous</a> with several <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estrus" title="Estrus" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBWI">estrus</a> cycles during a year, lasting usually 21 days. They are usually ready to mate between early February and August<sup about="#mwt643" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Jemmett1977_168-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Jemmett1977"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Jemmett1977-168"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Jemmett1977-168" id="mwBWM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBWQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWU">[</span>167<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWY">]</span></span></a></sup> in northern temperate zones and throughout the year in equatorial regions.<sup about="#mwt646" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-estrous_cycle_169-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"estrous_cycle"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-estrous_cycle-169"}}"><a href="#cite_note-estrous_cycle-169" id="mwBWc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBWg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWk">[</span>168<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBWo">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBWs">Several males, called tomcats, are attracted to a female in heat. They fight over her, and the victor wins the right to mate. At first, the female rejects the male, but eventually, the female allows the male to mate. The female utters a loud yowl as the male pulls out of her because a male cat's <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penis" title="Penis" id="mwBWw">penis</a> has a band of about 120–150 backward-pointing <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penile_spines" title="Penile spines" id="mwBW0">penile spines</a>, which are about <span about="#mwt647" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBW4" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"convert","href":"./Template:Convert"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"1"},"2":{"wt":"mm"},"3":{"wt":"in"},"abbr":{"wt":"on"},"4":{"wt":"2"}},"i":0}}]}">1</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt647"> </span><span about="#mwt647">mm (0.04</span><span typeof="mw:Entity" about="#mwt647"> </span><span about="#mwt647">in)</span> long; upon withdrawal of the penis, the spines may provide the female with increased sexual stimulation, which acts to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Induced_ovulation_(animals)" title="Induced ovulation (animals)" id="mwBW8">induce ovulation</a>.<sup about="#mwt650" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Aronson_1967_170-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Aronson 1967"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Aronson_1967-170"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Aronson_1967-170" id="mwBXA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBXE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBXI">[</span>169<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBXM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBXQ"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBXU"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg/250px-Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="1554" data-file-height="2321" data-file-type="bitmap" height="284" width="190" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg/500px-Radiography_of_a_pregnant_cat.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" id="mwBXY"></a><figcaption id="mwBXc">In this radiography of a pregnant cat, the skeletons of two fetuses are on the left and right of the uterus.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBXg">After mating, the female cleans her <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulva" title="Vulva" id="mwBXk">vulva</a> thoroughly. If a male attempts to mate with her at this point, the female attacks him. After about 20 to 30 minutes, once the female is finished grooming, the cycle will repeat.<sup about="#mwt651" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-compendium_171-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"compendium"}}"><a href="#cite_note-compendium-171" id="mwBXo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBXs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBXw">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBX0">]</span></span></a></sup> Because ovulation is not always triggered by a single mating, females may not be impregnated by the first male with which they mate.<sup about="#mwt654" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Wildt_1980_172-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Wildt 1980"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Wildt_1980-172"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Wildt_1980-172" id="mwBX4"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBX8"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYA">[</span>171<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYE">]</span></span></a></sup> Furthermore, cats are <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superfecundation" title="Superfecundation" id="mwBYI">superfecund</a>; that is, a female may mate with more than one male when she is in heat, with the result that different kittens in a litter may have different fathers.<sup about="#mwt657" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-compendium_171-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"compendium"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-compendium-171"}}"><a href="#cite_note-compendium-171" id="mwBYM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBYQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYU">[</span>170<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwBYc">The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morula" title="Morula" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBYg">morula</a> forms 124 hours after conception. At 148 hours, early <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blastocyst" title="Blastocyst" id="mwBYk">blastocysts</a> form. At 10–12 days, implantation occurs.<sup about="#mwt660" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-173" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-173"}}"><a href="#cite_note-173" id="mwBYo"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBYs"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBYw">[</span>172<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBY0">]</span></span></a></sup> The <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gestation" title="Gestation" id="mwBY4">gestation</a> of queens lasts between 64 and 67 days, with an average of 65 days.<sup about="#mwt661" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Jemmett1977_168-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Jemmett1977"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Jemmett1977-168" id="mwBY8"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBZA"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBZE">[</span>167<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBZI">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt664" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Tsutsui_1993_174-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Tsutsui 1993"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Tsutsui_1993-174"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Tsutsui_1993-174" id="mwBZM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwBZQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBZU">[</span>173<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwBZY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwBZc"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:പൂച്ചക്കുഞ്ഞുങ്ങൾ_(17_ദിവസം_പ്രായം).JPG" class="mw-file-description" id="mwBZg"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:പൂച്ചക്കുഞ്ഞുങ്ങൾ_(17_ദിവസം_പ്രായം).JPG" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9A%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9A%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%BE_%2817_%E0%B4%A6%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B5%E0%B4%B8%E0%B4%82_%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%82%29.JPG/250px-%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9A%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9A%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%BE_%2817_%E0%B4%A6%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B5%E0%B4%B8%E0%B4%82_%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%82%29.JPG" decoding="async" data-file-width="3360" data-file-height="2472" data-file-type="bitmap" height="184" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c9/%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9A%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9A%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%BE_%2817_%E0%B4%A6%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B5%E0%B4%B8%E0%B4%82_%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%82%29.JPG/500px-%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%82%E0%B4%9A%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9A%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%95%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%9E%E0%B5%81%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%99%E0%B5%BE_%2817_%E0%B4%A6%E0%B4%BF%E0%B4%B5%E0%B4%B8%E0%B4%82_%E0%B4%AA%E0%B5%8D%E0%B4%B0%E0%B4%BE%E0%B4%AF%E0%B4%82%29.JPG 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwBZk"></a><figcaption id="mwBZo">Two 17-day-old kittens</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwBZs">Based on a study of 2,300 free-ranging queens conducted from May 1998 and October<span class="nowrap" about="#mwt665" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwBZw" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Nbsp","href":"./Template:Nbsp"},"params":{},"i":0}}]}"><span typeof="mw:Entity"> </span></span>2000, they had one to six kittens per <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litter_(animal)" title="Litter (animal)" class="mw-redirect" id="mwBZ0">litter</a>, with an average of three kittens. They produced a mean of 1.4 litters per year, but a maximum of three litters in a year.
