<p id="mwB7s">In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt" title="Ancient Egypt" id="mwB7w">ancient Egypt</a>, cats were <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Animal_worship" title="Animal worship" id="mwB70">revered</a>. The goddess <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastet" title="Bastet" id="mwB74">Bastet</a> was often depicted in cat form, sometimes taking on the war-like aspect of a lioness. The Greek historian <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus" title="Herodotus" id="mwB78">Herodotus</a> reported that killing a cat was forbidden, and when a household cat died, the entire family mourned and shaved their eyebrows. Families took their dead cats to the sacred city of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bubastis" title="Bubastis" id="mwB8A">Bubastis</a>, where they were embalmed and buried in sacred repositories. Herodotus expressed astonishment at the domestic cats in Egypt, because he had only ever seen wildcats.<sup about="#mwt935" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Malek1997_249-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Malek1997"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Malek1997-249"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Malek1997-249" id="mwB8E"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB8I"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB8M">[</span>248<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB8Q">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwB8U">Ancient Greeks and Romans kept <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weasel" title="Weasel" id="mwB8Y">weasels</a> as pets, which were seen as the ideal rodent-killers. The earliest unmistakable evidence of the Greeks having domestic cats comes from two coins from <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Graecia" title="Magna Graecia" id="mwB8c">Magna Graecia</a> dating to the mid-fifth century BC showing Iokastos and Phalanthos, the legendary founders of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reggio_Calabria" title="Reggio Calabria" id="mwB8g">Rhegion</a> and <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taranto" title="Taranto" id="mwB8k">Taras</a> respectively, playing with their pet cats. The usual ancient Greek word for 'cat' was <span title="Ancient Greek (to 1453)-language text" about="#mwt936" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwB8o" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"grc-Latn"},"2":{"wt":"ailouros"}},"i":0}}]}"><i lang="grc-Latn">ailouros</i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Ancient_Greek_(to_1453)-language_text" about="#mwt936" id="mwB8s">, meaning 'thing with the waving tail'. Cats are rarely mentioned in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_literature" title="Ancient Greek literature" id="mwB8w">ancient Greek literature</a>. <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle" title="Aristotle" id="mwB80">Aristotle</a> remarked in his <i id="mwB84"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Animals" title="History of Animals" id="mwB88">History of Animals</a></i> that "female cats are naturally <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Promiscuity" title="Promiscuity" id="mwB9A">lecherous</a>". The Greeks later <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpretatio_graeca" title="Interpretatio graeca" id="mwB9E">syncretized</a> their own goddess <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis" title="Artemis" id="mwB9I">Artemis</a> with the Egyptian goddess Bastet, adopting Bastet's associations with cats and ascribing them to Artemis. In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ovid" title="Ovid" id="mwB9M">Ovid</a>'s <i id="mwB9Q"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metamorphoses" title="Metamorphoses" id="mwB9U">Metamorphoses</a></i>, when the deities flee to Egypt and take animal forms, the goddess <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_(mythology)" title="Diana (mythology)" id="mwB9Y">Diana</a> turns into a cat.<sup about="#mwt939" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Engels2001_250-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Engels2001"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Engels2001-250"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Engels2001-250" id="mwB9c"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB9g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB9k">[</span>249<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB9o">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt942" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-251" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-251"}}"><a href="#cite_note-251" id="mwB9s"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB9w"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB90">[</span>250<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB94">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwB98">Cats eventually displaced <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weasel" title="Weasel" id="mwB-A">weasels</a> as the pest control of choice because they were more pleasant to have around the house and were more enthusiastic hunters of mice. During the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages" title="Middle Ages" id="mwB-E">Middle Ages</a>, many of Artemis's associations with cats were grafted onto the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary,_mother_of_Jesus" title="Mary, mother of Jesus" id="mwB-I">Virgin Mary</a>. Cats are often shown in icons of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annunciation" title="Annunciation" id="mwB-M">Annunciation</a> and of the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Family" title="Holy Family" id="mwB-Q">Holy Family</a> and, according to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folklore_of_Italy" title="Folklore of Italy" id="mwB-U">Italian folklore</a>, on the same night that Mary gave birth to <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus" title="Jesus" id="mwB-Y">Jesus</a>, a cat in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bethlehem" title="Bethlehem" id="mwB-c">Bethlehem</a> gave birth to a kitten.<sup about="#mwt945" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Beadle1977_252-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Beadle1977"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Beadle1977-252"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Beadle1977-252" id="mwB-g"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB-k"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB-o">[</span>251<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB-s">]</span></span></a></sup> Domestic cats were spread throughout much of the rest of the world during the <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery" title="Age of Discovery" id="mwB-w">Age of Discovery</a>, as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship's_cat" title="Ship's cat" id="mwB-0">ships' cats</a> were carried on <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sailing_ship" title="Sailing ship" id="mwB-4">sailing ships</a> to control shipboard rodents and as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amulet" title="Amulet" id="mwB-8">good-luck charms</a>.<sup about="#mwt946" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Faure2009_44-1" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Faure2009"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Faure2009-44" id="mwB_A"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB_E"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB_I">[</span>43<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB_M">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwB_Q">Several ancient religions believed cats are exalted souls, companions or guides for humans, that are all-knowing but mute so they cannot influence decisions made by humans. In Japan, the <span title="Japanese-language text" about="#mwt947" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwB_U" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"lang","href":"./Template:Lang"},"params":{"1":{"wt":"ja-Latn"},"2":{"wt":"[[maneki neko]]"}},"i":0}}]}"><i lang="ja-Latn"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maneki_neko" title="Maneki neko" class="mw-redirect">maneki neko</a></i></span><link rel="mw:PageProp/Category" href="./Category:Articles_containing_Japanese-language_text" about="#mwt947" id="mwB_Y"> cat is a symbol of good fortune.<sup about="#mwt950" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-253" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-253"}}"><a href="#cite_note-253" id="mwB_c"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB_g"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB_k">[</span>252<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB_o">]</span></span></a></sup> In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_mythology" title="Norse mythology" id="mwB_s">Norse mythology</a>, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freyja" title="Freyja" id="mwB_w">Freyja</a>, the goddess of love, beauty, and fertility, is depicted as riding a chariot drawn by cats.<sup about="#mwt953" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-254" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-254"}}"><a href="#cite_note-254" id="mwB_0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwB_4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwB_8">[</span>253<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCAA">]</span></span></a></sup> In <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legends_of_the_Jews" title="Legends of the Jews" id="mwCAE">Jewish legend</a>, the first cat was living in the house of the first man <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adam" title="Adam" id="mwCAI">Adam</a> as a pet that got rid of <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mice" title="Mice" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCAM">mice</a>. The cat was once partnering with the first dog before the latter broke an oath they had made which resulted in enmity between the descendants of these two animals. It is also written that neither cats nor <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox" title="Fox" id="mwCAQ">foxes</a> are represented in the water, while every other animal has an incarnation species in the water.<sup about="#mwt956" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Ginzberg_255-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Ginzberg"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Ginzberg-255"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Ginzberg-255" id="mwCAU"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCAY"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCAc">[</span>254<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCAg">]</span></span></a></sup> Although no species are sacred in Islam, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_and_cats" title="Islam and cats" id="mwCAk">cats are revered by Muslims</a>. Some Western writers have stated <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad" title="Muhammad" id="mwCAo">Muhammad</a> had a favorite cat, <i id="mwCAs"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muezza" title="Muezza" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCAw">Muezza</a></i>.<sup about="#mwt959" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-256" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-256"}}"><a href="#cite_note-256" id="mwCA0"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCA4"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCA8">[</span>255<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCBA">]</span></span></a></sup> He is reported to have loved cats so much, "he would do without his cloak rather than disturb one that was sleeping on it".<sup about="#mwt962" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-Reeves_257-0" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{"name":"Reeves"},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-Reeves-257"}}"><a href="#cite_note-Reeves-257" id="mwCBE"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCBI"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCBM">[</span>256<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCBQ">]</span></span></a></sup> The story has no origin in early Muslim writers, and seems to confuse a story of a later <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sufi" title="Sufi" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCBU">Sufi</a> saint, <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmed_ar-Rifa'i" title="Ahmed ar-Rifa'i" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCBY">Ahmed ar-Rifa'i</a>, centuries after Muhammad.<sup about="#mwt965" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-258" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-258"}}"><a href="#cite_note-258" id="mwCBc"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCBg"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCBk">[</span>257<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCBo">]</span></span></a></sup> One of the companions of Muhammad was known as <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abu_Hurayrah" title="Abu Hurayrah" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCBs">Abu Hurayrah</a> ("father of the kitten"), in reference to his documented affection to cats.<sup about="#mwt968" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-259" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-259"}}"><a href="#cite_note-259" id="mwCBw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCB0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCB4">[</span>258<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCB8">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<section data-mw-section-id="40" id="mwCCA" aria-labelledby="Superstitions_and_rituals"><div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Superstitions_and_rituals">Superstitions and rituals</h3></div>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb" id="mwCCE"><a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_(1903)_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg" class="mw-file-description" id="mwCCI"><img resource="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_(1903)_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg" src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_%281903%29_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg/250px-Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_%281903%29_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg" decoding="async" data-file-width="7550" data-file-height="11861" data-file-type="bitmap" height="393" width="250" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8c/Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_%281903%29_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg/500px-Evelyn_De_Morgan_-_The_Love_Potion_%281903%29_-_Google_Cultural_Institute.jpg 2x" class="mw-file-element" id="mwCCM"></a><figcaption id="mwCCQ"><i id="mwCCU"><a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Love_Potion" title="The Love Potion" id="mwCCY">The Love Potion</a></i> is a 1903 painting by <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_De_Morgan" title="Evelyn De Morgan" id="mwCCc">Evelyn De Morgan</a> depicting a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Witch" title="Witch" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCCg">witch</a> with a black cat.</figcaption></figure>
<p id="mwCCk">Many cultures have negative <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superstition" title="Superstition" id="mwCCo">superstitions</a> about cats. For example, that encountering a <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_cat" title="Black cat" id="mwCCs">black cat</a> ("crossing one's path")<sup about="#mwt971" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-260" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-260"}}"><a href="#cite_note-260" id="mwCCw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCC0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCC4">[</span>259<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCC8">]</span></span></a></sup> leads to bad luck, or that cats are witches' <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Familiar_spirit" title="Familiar spirit" class="mw-redirect" id="mwCDA">familiar spirits</a> used to augment a witch's powers and skills. The killing of cats in medieval <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ypres" title="Ypres" id="mwCDE">Ypres</a>, Belgium, is commemorated in the innocuous present-day <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kattenstoet" title="Kattenstoet" id="mwCDI">Kattenstoet</a> (cat parade).<sup about="#mwt974" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-261" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-261"}}"><a href="#cite_note-261" id="mwCDM"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCDQ"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCDU">[</span>260<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCDY">]</span></span></a></sup></p>

<p id="mwCDc">According to a myth in many cultures, cats have multiple lives. In many countries, they are believed to have nine lives, but in Italy, Germany, Greece, Brazil, and some Spanish-speaking regions, they are said to have seven lives,<sup about="#mwt977" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-262" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-262"}}"><a href="#cite_note-262" id="mwCDg"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCDk"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCDo">[</span>261<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCDs">]</span></span></a></sup><sup about="#mwt980" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-263" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-263"}}"><a href="#cite_note-263" id="mwCDw"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCD0"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCD4">[</span>262<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCD8">]</span></span></a></sup> while in Arabic traditions, the number of lives is six.<sup about="#mwt983" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-264" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-264"}}"><a href="#cite_note-264" id="mwCEA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCEE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCEI">[</span>263<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCEM">]</span></span></a></sup> An early mention of the myth is in <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Heywood" title="John Heywood" id="mwCEQ">John Heywood</a>'s <i id="mwCEU">The Proverbs of John Heywood</i> (1546):<sup about="#mwt986" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-265" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-265"}}"><a href="#cite_note-265" id="mwCEY"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCEc"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCEg">[</span>264<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCEk">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r1244412712" typeof="mw:Extension/templatestyles mw:Transclusion" about="#mwt987" id="mwCEo" data-mw="{"name":"templatestyles","attrs":{"src":"Template:Blockquote/styles.css"},"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"Poem quote","href":"./Template:Poem_quote"},"params":{"text":{"wt":"Husband, ([[:wikt:quoth#Verb 2|quoth]] she), ye studie, be merrie now,\nAnd even as ye thinke now, so come to yow.\nNay not so, (quoth he), for my thought to tell right,\nI thinke how you lay [[:wikt:groning#English|groning]], wife, all last night.\nHusband, ''a groning horse and a groning wife''\n''Never faile their master'', (quoth she), for my life.\nNo wife, ''a woman [[:wikt:hath#English|hath]] nine lives like a cat''."}},"i":0}}]}">.mw-parser-output .templatequote{overflow:hidden;margin:1em 0;padding:0 32px}.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{line-height:1.5em;text-align:left;margin-top:0}@media(min-width:500px){.mw-parser-output .templatequotecite{padding-left:1.6em}}</style><blockquote class="templatequote " about="#mwt987" id="mwCEs"><div class="poem" typeof="mw:Extension/poem" about="#mwt989" id="mwCEw" data-mw="{"name":"poem","attrs":{},"body":{"extsrc":"Husband, ([[:wikt:quoth#Verb 2|quoth]] she), ye studie, be merrie now,\nAnd even as ye thinke now, so come to yow.\nNay not so, (quoth he), for my thought to tell right,\nI thinke how you lay [[:wikt:groning#English|groning]], wife, all last night.\nHusband, ''a groning horse and a groning wife''\n''Never faile their master'', (quoth she), for my life.\nNo wife, ''a woman [[:wikt:hath#English|hath]] nine lives like a cat''."}}"><p id="mwCE0">Husband, (<a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/quoth#Verb_2" title="wikt:quoth" class="extiw" id="mwCE4">quoth</a> she), ye studie, be merrie now,<br id="mwCE8">
And even as ye thinke now, so come to yow.<br id="mwCFA">
Nay not so, (quoth he), for my thought to tell right,<br id="mwCFE">
I thinke how you lay <a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/groning#English" title="wikt:groning" class="extiw" id="mwCFI">groning</a>, wife, all last night.<br id="mwCFM">
Husband, <i id="mwCFQ">a groning horse and a groning wife</i><br id="mwCFU">
<i id="mwCFY">Never faile their master</i>, (quoth she), for my life.<br id="mwCFc">
No wife, <i id="mwCFg">a woman <a rel="mw:WikiLink/Interwiki" href="https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/hath#English" title="wikt:hath" class="extiw" id="mwCFk">hath</a> nine lives like a cat</i>.</p></div></blockquote>

<p id="mwCFo">The myth is attributed to the natural suppleness and swiftness cats exhibit to escape life-threatening situations.<sup about="#mwt992" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-266" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-266"}}"><a href="#cite_note-266" id="mwCFs"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCFw"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCF0">[</span>265<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCF4">]</span></span></a></sup> Falling cats often land on their feet, using an instinctive <a rel="mw:WikiLink" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cat_righting_reflex" title="Cat righting reflex" id="mwCF8">righting reflex</a> to twist their bodies around.<sup about="#mwt995" class="mw-ref reference" id="cite_ref-267" rel="dc:references" typeof="mw:Extension/ref" data-mw="{"name":"ref","attrs":{},"body":{"id":"mw-reference-text-cite_note-267"}}"><a href="#cite_note-267" id="mwCGA"><span class="mw-reflink-text" id="mwCGE"><span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCGI">[</span>266<span class="cite-bracket" id="mwCGM">]</span></span></a></sup></p>
<div style="clear:both;" class="" about="#mwt996" typeof="mw:Transclusion" id="mwCGQ" data-mw="{"parts":[{"template":{"target":{"wt":"clear","href":"./Template:Clear"},"params":{},"i":0}}]}"></div>
